properties.name: Big Bone Lick
properties.title: Big Bone Lick
properties.subtitle: Boone County / salt lick & fossil beds
properties.history: Big Bone Lick was a mineral spring where Pleistocene mastodons, mammoths, and ground sloths left bones in the mud while seeking salt. Native peoples and later explorers—including Christopher Gist—collected fossils here; Thomas Jefferson later studied specimens from the lick. The site became Big Bone Lick State Historic Site, one of Kentucky’s earliest windows on deep time and a waypoint for salt hunters on the Ohio frontier.

properties.name: Lexington Named
properties.title: Lexington Named
properties.subtitle: Fayette County / McConnell Springs
properties.history: In early June 1775, William McConnell’s surveyors camped on a sinking spring of Elkhorn Creek when word arrived of the April 19 fight at Lexington, Massachusetts. They named the camp for that battle and returned east; permanent settlement waited until 1779, when Robert Patterson’s party built a blockhouse near present Main and Mill. Virginia established the town in 1782—the springs chose the site, the Revolution chose the name.

properties.name: Benjamin Logan / Logan's Station
properties.title: Benjamin Logan / Logan's Station
properties.subtitle: Lincoln County / St. Asaph near Stanford
properties.history: In 1775 Benjamin Logan left Boone's party and built Logan's Station (St. Asaph) near present-day Stanford—a stockade by Buffalo Spring that held through a roughly thirteen-day siege in May 1777. Logan hauled the wounded Burr Harrison inside under fire, then slipped out at night and walked about 150 miles to the Holston settlements for powder. He later helped write Kentucky's first constitution and settled on Bullskin Creek near Finchville in Shelby County.

properties.name: Shelbyville Founding
properties.title: Shelbyville Founding
properties.subtitle: Shelby County seat / Clear Creek
properties.history: Shelby County was carved from Jefferson County in 1792 and named for first governor Isaac Shelby. That October, at the first county court, Revolutionary veteran William Shannon donated about 50 acres on Clear Creek so the new seat would sit on the Frankfort-to-Falls road. Trustees required hewed-log houses with brick or stone chimneys; by 1800 the town had 262 people. Nearby Squire Boone's Painted Stone Station had been the earlier foothold—Shelbyville won the courthouse.

properties.name: Chickasaw / Jackson Purchase
properties.title: Chickasaw / Jackson Purchase
properties.subtitle: Western Kentucky / 1818 treaty
properties.history: West of the Tennessee River, Chickasaw hunting grounds stayed off Kentucky's settled map until October 19, 1818. Andrew Jackson and Isaac Shelby negotiated what became the Jackson Purchase: roughly 13,000 square miles (about 2,369 in Kentucky) for annuities. That treaty filled in the western counties from Ballard through McCracken and closed the last big Indigenous title claim inside the state.

properties.name: Frankfort Founding
properties.title: Frankfort Founding
properties.subtitle: Franklin County / Frank's Ford capital
properties.history: Before it was the capital, the site was a buffalo-trail ford on the Kentucky River. In 1780 pioneer Stephen Frank was killed in a skirmish there; settlers called the crossing Frank's Ford, which shortened to Frankfort. In 1786 Virginia chartered a town on land promoted by Gen. James Wilkinson. When Kentucky became a state in 1792, Frankfort outbid rivals for the capital, and Gideon Shryock's Greek Revival Old Capitol (1830) finally stuck after earlier buildings burned.

properties.name: Bullitt's Lick
properties.title: Bullitt's Lick
properties.subtitle: Bullitt County / Kentucky's first industry
properties.history: Salt was frontier white gold, and the only large commercial saltworks west of the Alleghenies during the Revolution sat about three miles west of present-day Shepherdsville. Capt. Thomas Bullitt surveyed the Salt River lick in 1773; production started in 1779 as workers boiled brine in rows of iron kettles. Pack trains and flatboats carried the salt across Kentucky, a fort went up in 1780, and a boomtown nicknamed Saltburg grew around the furnaces until cheaper salt arrived around 1830.

properties.name: George Rogers Clark / Corn Island
properties.title: George Rogers Clark / Corn Island
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County / Falls of the Ohio
properties.history: Virginia surveyor-turned-militia leader George Rogers Clark staged at Corn Island in the Falls of the Ohio in 1778, then launched the Illinois Campaign that took Kaskaskia and Vincennes from the British. The settlement he left behind became Louisville, chartered in 1780 and named for France’s Louis XVI. Fort Nelson later rose on the mainland as his western headquarters.

properties.name: Battle of Blue Licks
properties.title: Battle of Blue Licks
properties.subtitle: Robertson County · Aug 19, 1782 · largest Revolutionary battle in Kentucky
properties.history:
On August 19, 1782, a British and Native force under Capt. William Caldwell, mostly Wyandot and Great Lakes warriors with Butler's Rangers, ambushed about 180 Kentucky militia at the Lower Blue Licks on the Licking River.

Boone urged caution at the ford, but the militia crossed and attacked uphill. Within about fifteen minutes the line broke; roughly 60 to 77 Kentuckians were killed, including Col. John Todd, Lt. Col. Stephen Trigg and Boone's son Israel. A later tradition that Maj. Hugh McGary dared the men across is not in Boone's own accounts.

properties.name: Great Saltpetre Cave
properties.title: Great Saltpetre Cave
properties.subtitle: Rockcastle County / War of 1812 powder
properties.history: South of Mount Vernon in Rockcastle County, Great Saltpetre Cave was mined hard for calcium nitrate during the War of 1812, when British blockades cut off imported saltpeter for gunpowder. Dozens of workers (many enslaved) leached cave earth in wooden vats and shipped crystals to powder mills until trade reopened after 1815. The Rockcastle Karst Conservancy keeps the preserve today.

properties.name: Richard Henderson / Transylvania
properties.title: Richard Henderson / Transylvania
properties.subtitle: Henderson County / Transylvania Company
properties.history: North Carolina judge Richard Henderson reorganized his investors as the Transylvania Company in early 1775, then bargained at Sycamore Shoals for roughly 20 million acres between the Kentucky, Cumberland, and Ohio rivers. Cherokee headmen signed in mid-March; warrior Dragging Canoe opposed the sale and warned the country would become dark and bloody. Virginia later voided the private purchase but compensated the company with Ohio River acreage that seeded Henderson County.

properties.name: Bardstown Founding
properties.title: Bardstown Founding
properties.subtitle: Nelson County seat / Beech Fork
properties.history: The Bardstown area was explored in the mid-1770s and briefly called Salem. In 1780 William Bard surveyed a town on a 1,000-acre grant for his brother David and John Cockey Owings and set aside ground for public buildings. Named seat of new Nelson County in 1784, it was chartered by Virginia as Baird’s Town in 1788 and settled into the name Bardstown—one of Kentucky’s oldest inland towns.

properties.name: John Floyd / Floyd's Station
properties.title: John Floyd / Floyd's Station
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County / Beargrass Creek
properties.history: Virginia surveyor John Floyd led a 1774 Fincastle party into Kentucky, staked 2,000 acres on Beargrass Creek, and came back in 1779 to stockade Floyd's Station near today's St. Matthews. Virginia made him a Louisville trustee, Jefferson militia colonel, and in 1783 one of Kentucky's first two judges. On April 8 that year he rode toward Bullitt's Lick in a scarlet coat; a shot from ambush dropped him, and he died two days later at 32.

properties.name: Georgetown / Royal Spring
properties.title: Georgetown / Royal Spring
properties.subtitle: Scott County / Elijah Craig spring
properties.history: In July 1774 John Floyd claimed a thousand acres around a big Bluegrass spring. John McClelland built a cabin and stockade above it in 1775; an attack on December 29, 1776, killed McClelland, and the station emptied in 1777. Baptist preacher Elijah Craig later laid out Lebanon on the same spring, won a 1784 Virginia charter, and in 1790 renamed the place George Town for Washington. Scott County's seat still drinks from Royal Spring.

properties.name: Leestown
properties.title: Leestown
properties.subtitle: Franklin County / Kentucky River port
properties.history: In 1773 the McAfee company and Hancock Taylor surveyed a buffalo crossing on the Kentucky River about a mile north of today’s Frankfort. Hancock and Willis Lee planted a village on the north bank in 1775, the first Anglo-American settlement north of the river. Raids emptied it in 1777; it returned as a tobacco warehouse and shipping port for hemp, corn, and whiskey, and in 1827 limestone for the Old State House was quarried from the riverbank here.

properties.name: Squire Boone / Painted Stone / Long Run
properties.title: Squire Boone / Painted Stone / Long Run
properties.subtitle: Shelby & Jefferson counties / 1781 massacre
properties.history: Daniel's younger brother Squire Boone carved his name into a Clear Creek rock, painted the letters red, and by spring 1780 planted Shelby County's first large station about two miles north of present Shelbyville. After an April 1781 wound left Squire's right arm permanently short, most settlers fled toward Linn's Station and walked into the Long Run Massacre of September 13. He later rebuilt a mill on the burnt site before land debts cost him the station.

properties.name: Paris Founding
properties.title: Paris Founding
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County seat / 1789–1790
properties.history: Joseph Houston's 1776 station sat near Doyle Spring. Lawrence Protzman later platted 250 acres and in 1789 got Virginia to charter the town as Hopewell as Bourbon County's seat. In 1790 James Garrard and locals renamed it Paris to match the county, itself named for France's Bourbon kings who backed the Revolution. The post office briefly ran as Bourbonton before Paris stuck.

properties.name: Capt. Will Emery / Long Hunters
properties.title: Capt. Will Emery / Long Hunters
properties.subtitle: Warren County / hunting-ground conflict
properties.history: Shawnee held the larger northern and central Kentucky hunting grounds; Cherokee worked closer to Cumberland Gap. When long hunters stacked pelts for eastern markets, Native parties treated them as poachers. Around late 1769 a Shawnee band with Captain Will Emery took Boone and John Stewart’s six-month haul and warned them home: stay out, or the wasps and yellowjackets would sting. Not blank wilderness—a contested commons.

properties.name: Christopher Gist / Ohio Company
properties.title: Christopher Gist / Ohio Company
properties.subtitle: Fayette County / 1750–51 survey
properties.history: Fifteen-plus years before Boone’s fame, the Ohio Company hired surveyor Christopher Gist to probe the Ohio Valley down toward the Falls. Crossing into Kentucky, his journal logged rich bottomlands, canebrakes, buffalo plains, and Native towns. Shawnee at Lower Shawneetown warned him off the Falls; he brought the company a fossil “beest” tooth from Big Bone country and the first detailed English read of northeastern Kentucky.

properties.name: Jacob Spears
properties.title: Jacob Spears
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County / early bourbon whiskey
properties.history: Pennsylvania-born Revolutionary veteran Jacob Spears settled near Paris in Bourbon County and was distilling by the 1790s. Thomas Metcalfe built his stone house (“Stone Castle”) around 1790; the farm still holds a springhouse and whiskey storehouse—Kentucky’s most complete early distiller’s complex. Spears floated barrels down the Licking to the Ohio and on to New Orleans, and he is often credited among the first to market the county’s whiskey under the name that stuck: bourbon.

properties.name: John Filson
properties.title: John Filson
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County / Filson Club pin
properties.history: Pennsylvania schoolteacher and surveyor John Filson reached Lexington around 1783 with land warrants for more than 12,000 acres. In 1784 he published The Discovery, Settlement and Present State of Kentucke—the first written history of the country—with a companion map engraved in Philadelphia. The book’s appendix carried the earliest printed Boone narrative; in 1788 Filson helped plat Losantiville (later Cincinnati) and that October vanished while surveying near the Great Miami.

properties.name: Lexington & Ohio Railroad
properties.title: Lexington & Ohio Railroad
properties.subtitle: Franklin County / first KY railroad
properties.history: On January 27, 1830, Kentucky chartered the Lexington & Ohio—the commonwealth’s first railroad, and among the first west of the Alleghenies—to tie Lexington to the Ohio River. Track used English strap iron spiked to quarried limestone sills; horses pulled early cars, then steam. The “Daniel Boone” engine made Lexington to Frankfort in about two and a half hours in 1835, cracking open Bluegrass freight toward the river long before the Civil War.

properties.name: Bland W. Ballard / Tyler Station
properties.title: Bland W. Ballard / Tyler Station
properties.subtitle: Shelby County / Tick Creek
properties.history: Born Spotsylvania County, Va., October 16, 1761, Bland Williams Ballard came to Kentucky in 1779 and scouted for George Rogers Clark. With Robert Tyler he helped plant Tyler Station on Tick Creek east of Shelbyville around 1781. In 1788 Delaware warriors killed his father and several siblings near the station; Ballard fought through Fallen Timbers, survived capture at Frenchtown, represented Shelby County in the General Assembly, and died September 5, 1853. Ballard County carries his name.

properties.name: Gaitskill Mound
properties.title: Gaitskill Mound
properties.subtitle: Montgomery County / Adena tablets
properties.history: On Mount Sterling’s northern bypass, Gaitskill Mound is an Adena earthwork (roughly 800 B.C.–A.D. 700) listed on the National Register in 1975. Unlike many looted mounds, it yielded rare engraved stone and clay tablets recovered through University of Kentucky work associated with W.S. Webb—ritual objects tied to Adena cremation and mound ceremony rather than everyday trash. The site anchors Montgomery County’s deep Woodland past beneath the later townscape.

properties.name: James C. Crow / Oscar Pepper
properties.title: James C. Crow / Oscar Pepper
properties.subtitle: Woodford County / Labrot & Graham ground
properties.history: Scottish physician-chemist James C. Crow began advising Oscar Pepper's Woodford County farm still on Glenn's Creek by 1833. After Pepper rebuilt in stone (1837–38), Crow returned as master distiller (1840–55), measuring mash temperatures, yeast, and acidity with scientific care that fixed sour-mash practice as commercial habit. His whiskey shipped far beyond Kentucky; Old Crow later took his name, and the limestone valley still hosts Woodford Reserve on the old Pepper ground.

properties.name: Isaac Shelby
properties.title: Isaac Shelby
properties.subtitle: Lincoln County / Traveler's Rest
properties.history: Maryland-born Isaac Shelby fought at Point Pleasant, then helped lead the Overmountain Men to victory at Kings Mountain in 1780. He moved to Kentucky in the 1780s, helped push statehood, and in 1792 became the commonwealth's first governor; sixteen years later he returned as fifth governor and led militia at the Battle of the Thames. Shelby County still carries his name, and Traveler's Rest marks his home ground.

properties.title: William Whitley / Sportsman's Hill
properties.subtitle: Lincoln County / Crab Orchard
properties.history: Near Crab Orchard, William Whitley finished Sportsman's Hill (1787–1794), often called Kentucky's first brick house—thick walls, elevated windows, and hiding places against raids. Beside it he ran a clay oval where horses raced counter-clockwise, a pointed break from English turf clockwise. The house and hill remain a Lincoln County historic site.

properties.name: Estill's Defeat
properties.title: Estill's Defeat
properties.subtitle: Montgomery County / Little Mountain 1782
properties.history: On March 22, 1782, Capt. James Estill and about 25 Lincoln County militiamen overtook a Wyandot raiding party at Little Mountain Creek, near today’s Mount Sterling. After nearly two hours of fighting, Lt. William Miller’s left flank broke, the Wyandots closed, and Estill was killed in hand-to-hand combat along with six of his men. The fight—also called the Battle of Little Mountain—was one of the bloodiest single engagements of Kentucky’s “Year of Blood.”

properties.name: Cumberland Gap / Thomas Walker
properties.title: Cumberland Gap / Thomas Walker
properties.subtitle: Bell County / geologic doorway
properties.history: In March 1750 Dr. Thomas Walker led a Loyal Land Company party through the Appalachians and on April 13 recorded Cave Gap: a plain Indian road, a spring pouring from a cave, marked trees, and a pass visible for miles. He named the gap and nearby river for the Duke of Cumberland and later had a small cabin raised near present Barbourville—the first Euro-American house claimed in Kentucky. Walker’s journal mapped the geologic doorway later generations would pour through.

properties.name: Catherine Spears Carpenter
properties.title: Catherine Spears Carpenter
properties.subtitle: Casey County / 1818 sour-mash recipes
properties.history: Twice-widowed Catherine Spears Carpenter ran a large Casey County farm after 1806, raising crops, livestock, and surplus corn into whiskey. County tax records show her paying on 100 gallons of spirits in 1815. An 1818 manuscript in the Carpenter Family Papers preserves sweet-mash and sour-mash distilling recipes she used to instruct her household—one of the earliest written American sour-mash records, decades before James Crow’s fame.

properties.name: Wickliffe Mounds
properties.title: Wickliffe Mounds
properties.subtitle: Ballard County / Mississippian town
properties.history: Mississippian farmers founded Wickliffe around AD 1100 on a bluff over the Ohio, three miles from the Mississippi confluence. They built platform mounds, a plaza, houses, and after 1175 a cemetery mound; by 1350 the community capped its mounds and left. In the 1930s a promoter opened graves to tourists as “Ancient Buried City”; Murray State later professionalized the research, and the site became a state historic site in 2004.

properties.name: Falls of the Ohio
properties.title: Falls of the Ohio
properties.subtitle: Clarksville / Jefferson fossil beds
properties.history: About 390 million years ago a shallow Devonian sea laid down the Jeffersonville Limestone—coral banks and stromatoporoid sponges now exposed at the Falls of the Ohio. Those hard shelves made the only major rapids on the river, so flatboats had to portage; Louisville and the Indiana towns grew at that choke point. properties.name: Indian Knoll
properties.title: Indian Knoll
properties.subtitle: Late Archaic shell midden · Ohio County
properties.history:
About five thousand years ago, families in Ohio County kept coming back to the same patch of ground. They came for the freshwater mussels in the nearby shallows, and they stayed for the deer, turtles and nut trees. Each visit added to a growing mound of shell, ash and debris. Today we call it Indian Knoll, a shell midden that has become one of the best-known sites of the Archaic period in North America.

The people who lived here were hunters and gatherers, mainly during the Late Archaic (about 3000–1000 BCE). They did not stay in one place all year. They moved with the seasons, but they weren't wandering. Families planned each move using what they knew about when plants ripened, where animals went, and where to find stone and other supplies.

Mussels were a steady food source. They were full of protein, easy to collect, simple to cook, and could be gathered any time of year. The skeletons even suggest who gathered them. Women and children likely collected shellfish in shallow water.

Many men have bony growths in the inner ear, a condition that forms after repeated exposure to cold water, so men probably dove for mussels in deeper water. Most people were fairly healthy, but their teeth were badly worn. Sandstone pestles and nutting stones left tiny bits of grit in their food, which slowly ground down the enamel.

In the late 1930s, during the Depression, Works Progress Administration crews led by University of Kentucky archaeologists dug about 1.5 acres, roughly sixty percent of the site. They recorded hearths, roasting pits, burned clay floors and hundreds of human burials. They collected more than 50,000 artifacts, including spear points, bone pins, marine shell beads and bannerstones. The marine shell had traveled a long way to get here.

Some of the most moving finds were 23 dog burials. Archaic dogs were medium-sized, about 14 to 18 inches tall at the shoulder, and may have looked a little like wolves. Some dogs were buried in their own graves. Others were buried with adults or children.

People treated dogs in a way they treated no other animal. Their bones show they ate much the same food as people did.

## Kentucky today

In the early 1990s, Indian Knoll and nineteen other Late Archaic shell middens in the region were named National Historic Landmarks. The site is protected, and its location stays off public maps. Ohio County holds one of the deepest records we have of Archaic family life, including the dogs that lived alongside those families.

properties.history:
In Boone County, Cleek-McCabe is a thirteenth-century Fort Ancient village: a midden ring about 100 feet wide around a plaza about 200 feet across, with low burial mounds east and west. UK crews in the late 1930s sampled the ring and dug the western mound; the eastern mound still stands. Under that western mound they found three successive roofless public buildings—first a 43-foot circle, then rectangles up to about 56 by 95 feet—sharing a central pole pit that links Fort Ancient ritual architecture to earlier Adena and Hopewell submound screens.

Cordmarked jars with guilloche necks and triangular strap handles tie the pottery to Boone County and neighboring Ohio–Indiana Fort Ancient communities.

properties.name: Read Shell Midden (15Bt10)
properties.title: Read Shell Midden (15Bt10)
properties.subtitle: Butler County · Late Archaic shell midden
properties.history:
Long before farming came to Kentucky, Late Archaic people (roughly 3000–1000 BCE) came back to the same spots in Butler County year after year. Each visit added to a deep layer of shellfish shells, ash, broken tools and food waste. Archaeologists call these heaps shell middens. The Read Shell Midden is one of the best-recorded in the state.

It was a seasonal camp, and it was also a cemetery where families buried their dead in the same ground they had lived on.

The Archaic period was a time of hunting, fishing and gathering. Groups moved through the year to follow food sources: shellfish and fish in warm months, nuts and deer in the fall. A midden used again and again shows a deep tie to one place. Burying relatives there may have helped families claim that place as theirs.

From 1937 to 1939, crews paid by the Works Progress Administration dug the site under William S. Webb of the University of Kentucky. New Deal relief money paid unemployed Kentuckians to do the digging, and it built much of what scholars know about the state's ancient past. The crews recorded more than 240 burials. The bones were poorly preserved, so only about 152 individuals could be removed for study.

Webb published his report in 1950, and later researchers used the remains to study ancient age at death, health and population.

In 1986 the site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places as part of a group of Archaic shell middens. Together they make up Kentucky's densest Archaic shell-midden landscape.

properties.description:
Long before farming came to Kentucky, Late Archaic people (roughly 3000–1000 BCE) came back to the same spots in Butler County year after year. Each visit added to a deep layer of shellfish shells, ash, broken tools and food waste. Archaeologists call these heaps shell middens. The Read Shell Midden is one of the best-recorded in the state.

It was a seasonal camp, and it was also a cemetery where families buried their dead in the same ground they had lived on.

The Archaic period was a time of hunting, fishing and gathering. Groups moved through the year to follow food sources: shellfish and fish in warm months, nuts and deer in the fall. A midden used again and again shows a deep tie to one place. Burying relatives there may have helped families claim that place as theirs.

From 1937 to 1939, crews paid by the Works Progress Administration dug the site under William S. Webb of the University of Kentucky. New Deal relief money paid unemployed Kentuckians to do the digging, and it built much of what scholars know about the state's ancient past. The crews recorded more than 240 burials. The bones were poorly preserved, so only about 152 individuals could be removed for study.

Webb published his report in 1950, and later researchers used the remains to study ancient age at death, health and population.

properties.subtitle: Jessamine County · Early Fort Ancient Osborne Phase ~1010–1255 CE
properties.history:
University of Kentucky archaeologists dug the Muir site (15Js86) in Jessamine County. Radiocarbon and ceramics place it in the early Fort Ancient Osborne Phase, roughly 1010–1255 CE. Unlike later crowded plaza villages, Muir held only one to three rectangular single-set-post houses at a time, each with a shallow floor basin and central hearth—more a dispersed farmstead cluster than a stockaded town.

Residents ate mostly deer, elk, and bear, grew corn, beans, knotweed, and sunflower, and made limestone-tempered jars with rare guilloche designs.

properties.subtitle: Clark’s second-in-command · Harrodsburg petition 1776 · died 1779
properties.history: Virginia-born Joseph Bowman came to Kentucky by 1775, signed the 1776 Harrodsburg county petition, and in 1778 raised a company for George Rogers Clark. properties.history:
Frontiersman William Smeathers (Bill Smothers) built a cabin on the south bank of the Ohio in 1797 at a landing flatboat men already called Yellow Banks for its clay bluffs. Daviess County was created in 1815; the town was laid out in 1816 and incorporated in 1817 as Owensborough for Col. Abraham Owen, killed at Tippecanoe in 1811 (the spelling shortened later). Smothers later scouted for Stephen F. Austin's Old Three Hundred in Texas.

Downtown Smothers Park marks the home site — western Kentucky's river gate still sitting on that yellow bank.

properties.name: Turk Site (15Ce6)
properties.title: Turk Site (15Ce6)
properties.subtitle: Carlisle County · Mississippian Dorena–Medley
properties.history:
Between about 1100 and 1300 CE, a small community in Carlisle County built a planned town. It covered only about two and a half hectares, but its layout followed the pattern used across the Mississippian world: earthen platform mounds arranged around an open plaza. Mounds like these held up important buildings, such as the houses of leaders or community structures. The plaza was where people gathered for ceremonies, games and public life.

Archaeologists place most of the town's history in what they call the Dorena phase (about 1100–1300 CE), and some people stayed on into the later Medley phase. That was a time of big changes in the Ohio Valley. Farming communities that grew corn were organizing into chiefdoms. Many were small towns tied to larger centers through trade, marriage and shared religious ideas.

Building mounds took organized labor over many seasons, so a planned town this size suggests leaders who could call on their neighbors to help. It also suggests a community that wanted its place in that wider world to be visible on the land.

People may also have moved here from an older settlement elsewhere in the county. That kind of move was common in the Mississippian period, when towns were founded, enlarged and abandoned as politics, farmland and alliances shifted. By the 1400s, many Mississippian towns in the region had been left behind.

The site first appeared in print in the 1880s. The most thorough modern investigation was Richard Edging's work, published in 1985, which is still the main reference for its chronology and layout.

## Kentucky today

The site is protected, and its exact location is kept out of public view to guard against looting. Like other Mississippian places in Carlisle County, it shows that western Kentucky was home to organized farming towns centuries before Europeans arrived. The best way to honor it is from a distance: learn about it, and support the archaeologists and descendant communities who look after places like it.

properties.title: David Snowden homeplace
properties.subtitle: Lee County · St. Helens · Middle Fork Kentucky River
properties.history:
Historic Snowden homeplace near St. Helens (Lee County), on a knob by the Middle Fork Kentucky River (KY 52 east of Beattyville). David Snowden Sr. (1759 near Perth Amboy, N.J. – 1839 Estill Co.) served as a Revolutionary War frontier “Indian spy” and guard from Washington Co., Pa. (federal pension W9308), and also on Gen. Lachlan McIntosh’s 1778 Ohio campaign and Col. William Crawford’s 1782 Sandusky expedition; he married Nancy Hazelrigg in 1782. His son David Snowden Jr. (1786–1852) built a log cabin, kitchen, and quarters here about 1825; a later two-story clapboard house on sandstone had a wing that served as the St. Helens post office.

The family also appears in Owsley County around 1850 before Lee County split. The abandoned house was photographed extensively and was reportedly demolished after a fire. Photos: https://abandonedonline.net/location/david-snowden-house/ and https://abandonedonline.net/david-snowden-jrs-house/ . Pension abstract: https://kygenweb.net/estill/site/records/military/revwar/snowden01.htm.

He sold only "H. McKenna Old Line" sour mash—never green whisky under three years—and stamped barrels with an Irish harp. The brand later survived Prohibition as medicinal whisky; Heaven Hill revived it in the modern era.

properties.name: Estill Springs
properties.title: Estill Springs
properties.subtitle: Estill County · Irvine · KY 89 (marker 555)
properties.history:
Mineral springs about half a mile north of Irvine on today’s KY 89, long known to Shawnee camps and early Kentucky explorers (Boone, Boyle, McAfee, and others). Operated as a resort from 1814 until the hotel burned in 1924; white sulphur water, Sweet Lick Knob views, and a popular ballroom drew visitors from across the state.

In 1861 owner Col. Sidney M. Barnes organized the 8th Kentucky Infantry (USA) here; the grounds later hosted Confederate reunions of Morgan’s men, including the last. Kentucky Historical Society marker #555 stands on Main Street across from Estill Springs Elementary. Historic photo (c. 1910): https://scholarworks.moreheadstate.edu/sprague_photo_collection/117/

properties.name: John Finley
properties.title: John Finley
properties.subtitle: Eskippakithiki trade ~1752 · Boone expedition guide 1769 · Clark County
properties.history: Long before Wilderness Road fame, Pennsylvania-born trader John Finley (also Findley) was crossing the Alleghenies for furs. Around 1752 he reached Eskippakithiki, the Shawnee town in today’s Clark County, one of the earliest recorded Euro-American trading trips into central Kentucky. Years later, as a Braddock-campaign acquaintance of Daniel Boone, he returned to the Yadkin with stories of cane-rich hunting grounds beyond Cumberland Gap. In May 1769 he guided Boone’s party through that gap; Finley’s firsthand routes—not Boone alone—helped open the country settlers would soon claim.

properties.name: Springfield / Washington County seat
properties.title: Springfield / Washington County seat
properties.subtitle: First county after statehood 1792 · town laid out 1793 · Matthew Walton
properties.history:
Washington County was the first county the new Kentucky legislature created after 1792 statehood, named for George Washington. In 1793 a site near the old Wilderness Trace was chosen for the seat on land tied to Gen. Matthew Walton; surveyor David Caldwell laid out the public square, and the town took the name Springfield.

Early stations—Sandusky (1776), Cartwright’s (1778)—and Parker’s Landing on Beech Fork had already drawn settlers from the Gap road; Maryland Catholics arrived in force from 1785. The Lincoln family later settled nearby on Beech Fork, and Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks’s marriage bond still sits in the Washington County clerk’s office.

properties.name: Ruddell's Station
properties.title: Ruddell's Station
properties.subtitle: Harrison County · fort 1779 · Bird capture June 1780 · South Fork Licking
properties.history:
In spring 1779 Capt. Isaac Ruddell rebuilt a fort on the South Fork of Licking (Harrison County) on the old Hinkson site—Ruddell’s Station, or Fort Liberty—soon joined by many Pennsylvania German families. In June 1780 British Capt. Henry Bird marched south with cannon, Canadian volunteers, and hundreds of Native allies. Artillery cracked the log walls; Ruddell surrendered under a promise of protection, then watched the agreement collapse as roughly four hundred captives were marched toward Detroit.

Two of his sons were adopted by Shawnee; Stephen later lived as Tecumseh’s companion. The British never again brought that scale of artillery into Kentucky.

properties.name: Simpsonville
properties.title: Simpsonville
properties.subtitle: Shelby County · laid out 1816 · Capt. John Simpson namesake
properties.history:
In Shelby County, Isaac Watkins petitioned to lay out Simpsonville in 1816 as a waystation on the Louisville–Shelbyville road. A post office opened in 1821; the town incorporated in 1833. It was named for Capt. John Simpson, a Shelby County lawyer and Speaker of the Kentucky House (1810–11) who fought at Fallen Timbers (1794), won a seat in Congress in 1812, then died at the River Raisin on January 22, 1813.

By the mid-1820s the place was a busy Midland Trail stage stop — home ground for anyone driving US 60 past Bagdad today.

properties.name: Saltpeter Cave (Carter Caves)
properties.title: Saltpeter Cave (Carter Caves)
properties.subtitle: Carter County · War of 1812 niter mining · 15Cr99
properties.history: In Carter County’s Carter Caves State Resort Park, Saltpeter Cave (15Cr99) was mined for potassium nitrate during the War of 1812, when British blockades forced Americans to scrape gunpowder ingredients from their own caves. University of Kentucky archaeologists in the early 1990s documented impressions and remnants of 26 wooden leaching vats — a hybrid of big-box and small V-shaped cottage setups with wooden piping. Kentucky caves yielded more than 300,000 pounds of saltpeter statewide; this one is on the National Register and open for summer tours.

properties.name: Jenny Wiley / Big Sandy
properties.title: Jenny Wiley / Big Sandy
properties.subtitle: Captivity & escape 1789–1790 · Johnson Co. settlement 1800
properties.history:
On October 1, 1789, at Walker's Creek in present-day Bland County, Virginia, a Cherokee–Shawnee party seeking revenge on Matthias Harman mistakenly hit Thomas Wiley's cabin. Jenny (Virginia Sellards) Wiley saw her brother and three children killed; she and an infant were taken captive.

Over nearly eleven months in the Big Sandy country the infant died and another child born in captivity was killed. She escaped by following a dream-path of creeks to Harman's Station near present-day Paintsville, where men built a log raft and pulled her across. Reunited with Thomas in Virginia, the couple settled on Tom's Creek in what became Johnson County in 1800; she died there in 1831. Jenny Wiley State Resort Park on Dewey Lake near Prestonsburg carries her name.

properties.name: Buckner Site (15Bb12)
properties.title: Buckner Site (15Bb12)
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County · Fort Ancient occupation ~1200–1550 CE
properties.history: In Bourbon County, the Buckner Site (15Bb12) holds two circular Fort Ancient villages around central plazas, occupied mainly about A.D. 1200–1400 and into the early 1500s. Wall-trench houses, shell- and limestone-tempered pottery, triangular points, and a stone-paved McCray Mound mortuary area show maize farmers tied into Ohio Valley exchange. University of Kentucky WPA crews dug there in 1939; later work mapped the rings. It was listed on the National Register in 1983 (address restricted) — Bluegrass country that was already a settled farming landscape centuries before the county’s later towns.

properties.name: McGary's Station / Shawnee Springs
properties.title: McGary's Station / Shawnee Springs
properties.subtitle: Mercer County · station ~1779 · McGary at Blue Licks 1782
properties.history:
Irish-born Hugh McGary (1744–1806) came into Kentucky in 1775 with Boone's party, settled near Fort Harrod, and built McGary's Station around 1779 at Shawnee Springs in today's Mercer County. On August 19, 1782, as a major under Col. John Todd, he commanded the center at Blue Licks.

Boone urged caution at the Licking ford, but the militia crossed into an ambush; a later tradition, not in Boone's own accounts, says McGary dared the men across. In the rout roughly seventy Kentuckians fell in minutes, including Todd and Israel Boone. McGary survived—and later killed the surrendered Shawnee chief Moluntha on Logan's 1786 Ohio raid, earning a court-martial suspension.

properties.name: Bagdad / Consolation rail stop
properties.title: Bagdad / Consolation rail stop
properties.subtitle: Shelby County · L&F Railroad ~1850 · post office 1861
properties.history:
Northeastern Shelby County's Bagdad grew because the Louisville and Frankfort Railroad reached the area about 1850. Earlier settlers clustered at Consolation, roughly a mile east, with a post office from 1849; once the depot and mill sat on the line, people drifted west and Consolation faded.

On October 12, 1861, the Christiansburg post office moved to the station and took the name Bagdad, with Richard Radford as first postmaster. The place became a shipping point for flour, meal, livestock, and tobacco. Bagdad still sits at KY 12 and 395, about eleven miles northeast of Shelbyville.

properties.name: Holder's Station / Lower Howard's Creek
properties.title: Holder's Station / Lower Howard's Creek
properties.subtitle: Clark County · station ~1782 · KY River flatboat hub
properties.history:
John Holder (1753–1799) came to Kentucky in 1777, fought under George Rogers Clark, and commanded Fort Boonesborough in 1779. In 1782 he planted Holder's Station about a mile downstream from Boonesborough on the north bank of the Kentucky River, near the mouth of Lower Howard's Creek in what became Clark County. The stockade grew into a store, tavern, ferry, warehouse, mill, and boatyard—a Kentucky River flatboat hub for New Orleans-bound produce and one of the Bluegrass's earliest industrial corridors.

He married Fanny Callaway (one of the girls captured with Jemima Boone in 1776), sat as a Clark County justice under Governor Isaac Shelby, and is remembered on Kentucky Historical Marker 1048 and the John Holder Trail at Lower Howard's Creek Nature & Heritage Preserve.

properties.title: Lebanon / Hardin's Creek Meeting House
properties.subtitle: Marion County · meeting house 1789 · town 1814–15 · seat 1834
properties.history: Lebanon grew around Hardin's Creek Meeting House, a Presbyterian congregation Virginia settlers planted in 1789. The town was formally established in 1814, incorporated in 1815, and named for the biblical Lebanon because of the cedar timber on nearby hills. It sat first in Nelson County, then Washington after 1792; when Marion County was cut from Washington in 1834, Lebanon became the seat—named for South Carolina's Revolutionary "Swamp Fox," Francis Marion. The early church nucleus still marks the center of Marion County's map.

properties.name: Sweet Lick Knob Fort Ancient public building
properties.title: Sweet Lick Knob Fort Ancient public building
properties.subtitle: Estill County · Fort Ancient public building ~1400–1450 CE
properties.history:
Sometime around 1400 CE, Fort Ancient people in Estill County built a very large building. It wasn't a house. It stood about 42 feet long and 28 feet wide, with more than 1,176 square feet of floor. Down its center ran a line of three deep pits where tall poles had once stood, and two neat rectangular hearths.

For about fifty years, until about 1450, this building seems to have been a place where people came together.

The Fort Ancient people were farmers who lived in the middle Ohio Valley from about 1000 CE until after Europeans arrived. Most of them lived in villages that were often circular, with houses ringed around a plaza. A single large public building with no village plan around it is unusual. University of Kentucky archaeologists dug the site in 2010.

They studied the building's size, what was inside it, what was found on its floor, and its radiocarbon dates, and concluded that it was a public building for social or ritual meetings that happened from time to time.

The pole pits tell part of the story. Each was about a foot and a half across and went more than two feet below the floor. Poles like these may have held sacred meaning.

At some point, the southern hearth and the southern pole pit were capped with clay at the same moment. This looks like a deliberate act, perhaps closing one part of the building's life.

People also worked here. The floor held every stage of making sandstone disks: rough stones chipped into circles, chipped again to make them smaller, then ground smooth. Disks like these may have been used in games such as chunkey. The floor also held ornaments made of cannel coal, a shiny coal found in eastern Kentucky.

The site lies where two kinds of Fort Ancient country meet. To the east, most sites from this time are rockshelters, used by people who traveled and hunted in the mountains. To the west, most are large villages. Archaeologists think the hill itself, which can be seen from far away, may have worked like a beacon, drawing scattered groups together for ceremonies.

## Kentucky today

The site is protected, and its exact location stays off public maps to guard it from looting. It reminds us that Fort Ancient life in Estill County included more than farms and villages: there were also shared places where separate communities met. Learn about it from a distance, and support the archaeologists and descendant nations who look after places like it.

properties.name: Falmouth at the Licking Forks
properties.title: Falmouth at the Licking Forks
properties.subtitle: Pendleton County · town 1793 · county seat from 1799
properties.history:
Falmouth was established in 1793 at the confluence of the Main Licking and South Licking in what became Pendleton County. Virginians who settled there named it for Falmouth in Stafford County, Virginia. Pendleton County was formed in 1798 from parts of Bracken and Campbell (organized 1799) and named for Virginia statesman Edmund Pendleton; Falmouth has been the county seat ever since.

The forks made the spot a natural river landing—Colonel Henry Bird's 1780 British–Indian expedition passed this way toward Ruddell's and Martin's Stations—and the town still sits where those two Licking branches meet, about thirty-nine miles south of Cincinnati.

properties.name: Worthington's Fort (Edward Worthington)
properties.title: Worthington's Fort (Edward Worthington)
properties.subtitle: Boyle County · fort ~1779 · 4 mi SE of Danville
properties.history:
Irish-born Edward Worthington (c. 1754–1804) reached the Kentucky country as a surveyor on Beargrass Creek by 1775, fought in Lord Dunmore's War, and was wounded defending McClelland's Station against Mingo warriors under Pluggy on December 29, 1776. As a captain and paymaster under George Rogers Clark he helped take Vincennes (1779), then planted Worthington's Fort about four miles southeast of present Danville.

In 1780 Clark ordered his company to build Fort Jefferson on the Chickasaw Bluffs near the Ohio–Mississippi confluence; continuous Chickasaw pressure forced its abandonment in 1781. Worthington later died of yellow fever in New Orleans while chasing a land-fraud suit.

properties.name: Fort Jefferson (Clark's post on the Mississippi)
properties.title: Fort Jefferson (Clark's post on the Mississippi)
properties.subtitle: Ballard County · Virginia post 1780–1781 · Worthington's company
properties.history:
In 1780 George Rogers Clark ordered Capt. Edward Worthington's company of the Illinois Regiment to occupy the bluffs just below the Ohio–Mississippi confluence and build Fort Jefferson, anchoring Virginia's claim to the Mississippi and guarding Illinois County against river-borne threats from the south. Settler families joined a small civil town (Clarksville) beside the post, but the fort sat on Chickasaw land without their consent; continuous Chickasaw pressure, sickness, and short supplies made it indefensible, and Worthington withdrew the garrison and abandoned it in 1781.

Fort Jefferson Hill at Wickliffe, with its memorial cross above the confluence, marks the vicinity today (KHS marker 1309, Fort Jefferson Site).

properties.name: Paducah — 1827 William Clark plat
properties.title: Paducah — 1827 William Clark plat
properties.subtitle: McCracken County · platted 1827 · incorporated 1830 · seat 1832
properties.history:
After the 1818 Jackson Purchase opened Chickasaw land west of the Tennessee River, a small landing called Pekin grew at the Ohio–Tennessee confluence. In 1827 William Clark (of Lewis and Clark, then Superintendent of Indian Affairs) platted a town on that ground and named it Paducah for the Padouca, a people he had known on the plains and believed nearly erased by European expansion—not the later folk legend of a Chickasaw "Chief Paduke."

The town incorporated in 1830 and became McCracken County's seat in 1832, riding steamboat traffic into a river-and-rail hub.

properties.name: Slack Farm (15Un28) Caborn-Welborn village
properties.title: Slack Farm (15Un28) Caborn-Welborn village
properties.subtitle: Union County · Caborn-Welborn village ~1400–1700 CE
properties.history:
In the fall of 1987, the Kentucky Heritage Council learned that people were looting a village site in Union County. Ten men had leased the right to dig there. They tore open hundreds of graves to search for pots and beads to sell. The damage horrified people across the country, and Slack Farm became a turning point in how the United States protects Native graves.

The village had a long history before that. Slack Farm was a large community of the Caborn-Welborn culture, a late Mississippian people of the lower Ohio Valley, occupied from about 1400 to 1700 CE. Sidney S. Lyon recorded it for the Smithsonian Institution in 1868, but it got little professional attention after that until the looting.

It covered about 75 acres. At least seven residential areas each had their own storage pits and cemeteries. Six were grouped around a plaza or a series of courtyards, and graves were often laid out in parallel rows facing the plaza. Houses were shallow basins with wattle-and-daub walls, made of woven wooden strips plastered with clay.

Each house had a clay hearth. When families left a house, they broke their old cooking and serving pots and left them in the hearth. Storage pits more than six feet wide and six feet deep held dried food. Some had sprouted corn, a sign that part of the stored crop had spoiled.

One full pit may have fed seven to twelve people for a year. Jars carried trailed and incised triangles that archaeologists read as sun symbols.

Slack Farm was connected to faraway places. Catlinite and non-local pottery came from the north. Central Mississippi Valley pots, Nodena arrowheads and marine shell came from the southwest. After about 1550, glass beads and ornaments cut from European copper and brass kettles arrived through Native trade networks, before any European is known to have visited.

In early 1988, archaeologists from the Heritage Council, the University of Kentucky and Indiana University, along with several hundred volunteers, documented more than 450 looter holes. They recorded more than 300 burials in seven cemetery areas. Forensic study found the looters had disturbed at least 850 people. Those remains were then reburied at the site.

## Kentucky today

Public outrage over Slack Farm helped push Kentucky and other states to strengthen their grave-protection laws. It also helped build support for the federal Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act of 1990. The site is protected, and its location stays off public maps. Union County's lesson is simple: these are graves, not treasure.

properties.name: Craig's Station / Travelling Church (Gilbert's Creek)
properties.title: Craig's Station / Travelling Church (Gilbert's Creek)
properties.subtitle: Garrard County · Travelling Church arrives Dec 1781 · near Lancaster
properties.history:
In fall–winter 1781, Rev. Lewis Craig led roughly 200 Baptists and about 400 other settlers from Spotsylvania County, Virginia—the largest single pioneer party yet to enter the Kentucky District. Capt. William Ellis guided the train through Cumberland Gap; they raised a fortified meetinghouse and Craig's Station at Gilbert's Creek (near present Lancaster) that December. Members later founded Gilbert's Creek Baptist (still active), South Elkhorn, Clear Creek, and other congregations that seeded central Kentucky's Baptist landscape.

Lewis's brother Elijah stayed behind in Virginia awhile to press for religious liberty with James Madison before following west.

properties.name: Hubbell's Flatboat Fight — Limestone Landing
properties.title: Hubbell's Flatboat Fight — Limestone Landing
properties.subtitle: Mason County · Ohio River flatboat stand, March 23 1791 · landed at Limestone (Maysville)
properties.history:
On March 23, 1791, Capt. William Hubbell of the Frankfort frontier was taking a flatboat down the Ohio toward Limestone (today’s Maysville) with Daniel Light, William Plascut’s family, and others—about twenty souls after late pickups. At dawn near the Kanawha country, three Indian canoes closed in. Hubbell’s nine armed men held a running fight; he kept firing after a ball wrecked his gun lock, used a firebrand to touch off another shot, then drove boarders back with pistols and firewood even after a bullet tore his right arm.

Two of his men died in the boat, another later at Limestone; the women and children survived. The party reached Limestone that night. A companion boat under Capt. Greathouse, which had not prepared to fight, was taken ashore with grim results.

properties.name: Augusta founding / Capt. Philip Buckner
properties.title: Augusta founding / Capt. Philip Buckner
properties.subtitle: Bracken County · 600-acre town grant 1797 · early county seat
properties.history: Captain Philip Buckner, a Revolutionary War commissary officer with Virginia land grants in what became Bracken County, gave 600 acres to lay out Augusta in 1797. The Kentucky legislature chartered the river town that October; Augusta served as Bracken’s early county seat. Buckner later sat in the 1799 constitutional convention and the legislature, and lived many years at Woodlawn before dying in 1830. Augusta’s Ohio-River landing put northeastern Kentucky on a main corridor between Limestone and Cincinnati long before Covington filled the Licking Point.

properties.name: Egushawa's Odawa at Martin's Station
properties.title: Egushawa's Odawa at Martin's Station
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County · Odawa war chief with Bird's invasion · Martin's Station 1780 · Greenville 1795
properties.history:
Egushawa (also Au-goosh-away), the Detroit-area Odawa war chief often treated as Pontiac’s successor, helped Britain recruit Wabash and Great Lakes allies against Kentucky settlements. In 1780 he led an Ottawa contingent with Capt. Henry Bird’s cannon-backed invasion that forced the surrenders at Ruddell’s and Martin’s stations and marched hundreds of prisoners north toward Detroit.

After 1783 he rejected land cessions made without tribal consent, fought in the Northwest Confederacy’s victories over Harmar and St. Clair, was wounded at Fallen Timbers in 1794, and signed Greenville in 1795 as a principal Ottawa spokesman—tying Odawa strategy on the Maumee and Detroit to the raids that shaped Kentucky’s last Revolutionary decade.

properties.name: Cloudsplitter Rockshelter (15Mf36)
properties.title: Cloudsplitter Rockshelter (15Mf36)
properties.subtitle: Menifee County · Late Archaic squash and early plant tending
properties.history:
In Menifee County, Cloudsplitter Rockshelter holds a deep Archaic-to-Early Woodland record. Dry sand preserved a roughly 3,700-year-old squash rind—early evidence that people here were tending plants—as well as chipped and ground stone tools and pollen that tracks climate change.

Later Woodland layers at Cloudsplitter and neighboring Menifee County shelters (Newt Kash, Haystack, Rogers) show storage pits, seed crops such as sunflower, sumpweed, maygrass, and knotweed, and a shift from nut-heavy foraging toward small-scale gardens. These dry shelters are why eastern Kentucky figures so largely in the story of plant domestication in eastern North America.

properties.name: Ephraim McDowell House — first ovariotomy (1809)
properties.title: Ephraim McDowell House — first ovariotomy (1809)
properties.subtitle: Boyle County · Danville · Jane Todd Crawford surgery, Dec 25 1809
properties.history:
On Christmas Day 1809 in Danville, Dr. Ephraim McDowell—Scotch-Irish, Edinburgh-trained, practicing on the Kentucky frontier since 1795—removed a 22.5-pound ovarian tumor from Jane Todd Crawford of Greensburg. She had ridden roughly sixty miles believing she was overdue in pregnancy; McDowell diagnosed a cyst and operated in his home without anesthesia or antisepsis while assistants held her. The surgery lasted about twenty-five minutes.

Crawford recovered and lived more than three decades more. McDowell’s later reports helped prove that opening the abdomen need not be a death sentence, making Danville a landmark in the history of surgery west of the Alleghenies.

properties.name: Mary Ingles at Big Bone Lick (1755 escape)
properties.title: Mary Ingles at Big Bone Lick (1755 escape)
properties.subtitle: Boone County · Shawnee captive at the salt camp · escape ~mid-Oct 1755 · KHS marker
properties.history:
In July 1755 a Shawnee war party struck Draper's Meadow on the Virginia frontier and carried Mary Draper Ingles, then about twenty-three and pregnant, west with her two young sons. After the long march to the Ohio villages she was put to work at a salt-making camp at Big Bone Lick in what is now Boone County—among the earliest recorded European women on Kentucky ground.

Around mid-October she slipped away with an older Dutch captive woman and walked the Ohio, Kanawha, and New River corridors for roughly forty-two days, foraging on walnuts, grapes, and roots until she reached a New River cabin near her old home. Her son Thomas was later ransomed; she lived until 1815. The Kentucky Historical Society marker at Big Bone Lick still marks the breakout that turned a captivity story into one of the frontier's great return journeys.

properties.name: Bowling Green founding / Bolin Green (1798)
properties.title: Bowling Green founding / Bolin Green (1798)
properties.subtitle: Warren County seat · Robert & George Moore land · Fountain Square · town laid out 1798
properties.history:
Long hunters marked the Barren River country in 1775; McFadden's Station rose on the north bank in 1778. In the mid-1790s brothers Robert and George Moore settled by a big spring, and when Warren County was created they donated land for a log courthouse and jail—today's Fountain Square.

On more than thirty additional acres the county court laid out a town in early 1798 and named it Bolin Green, recalling New York's Bowling Green where patriots had pulled down King George's statue. The settlement won the county seat in 1809 and incorporated in 1812, growing into south-central Kentucky's commercial hub on the river and later the Louisville & Nashville road.

properties.name: E.H. Taylor Jr. / Old Taylor Distillery — Bottled-in-Bond Act (1897)
properties.title: E.H. Taylor Jr. / Old Taylor Distillery — Bottled-in-Bond Act (1897)
properties.subtitle: Franklin County · Millville (Glenn's Creek) · Taylor's castle distillery · Bottled-in-Bond Act signed Mar 3 1897
properties.history:
Colonel Edmund Haynes Taylor Jr. (1830–1923) of Frankfort rebuilt Kentucky whiskey's reputation after the Civil War—raising the O.F.C. (Old Fire Copper) plant in 1869, later the Old Taylor works on Glenn's Creek, and fighting the flood of adulterated "rectified" spirits. Working with Treasury Secretary John G. Carlisle, he helped push the Bottled-in-Bond Act, signed March 3, 1897: one distiller, one distillery, one season; at least four years in wood under federal lock; bottled at 100 proof with nothing added but water.

It was among the nation's first consumer-protection laws for spirits, and the green bond stamp became the buyer's guarantee that what was in the bottle was straight whiskey—not prune juice and industrial alcohol.

properties.name: Singer-Hieronymus Site Complex (15Sc3 / 15Sc225)
properties.title: Singer-Hieronymus Site Complex (15Sc3 / 15Sc225)
properties.subtitle: Scott County · circular Fort Ancient villages ~1200–1550
properties.history:
In Scott County, one Fort Ancient community kept moving its village, and the ground still shows where every one stood. Each time people moved, they built a new ring of houses around an open plaza, a short walk from the last one. Over the centuries those moves left a cluster of circular villages unlike any other known in Kentucky or anywhere else in the Fort Ancient world.

University of Kentucky archaeologists first studied the site in the 1920s, when they recorded two circular villages. They came back in the late 1990s. In the late 2010s, teams from East Tennessee State University and the University of Alabama joined them. Fieldwork over many seasons has now documented at least six villages.

Each village shows up as a "midden stain," a ring of dark soil made by everyday life. The rings follow the same plan. Houses stood in a band around the plaza. People buried their dead in front of their houses, close to the plaza.

They threw most of their trash out behind their homes. Five of the stains date from about 1300 to 1400 CE, and one dates to the 1500s. The community may have grown and shrunk as families arrived or moved away, and at times more than one village may have stood at once.

The largest ring, Midden Stain C, covers more than two and a half acres. It is about 330 feet across, with a plaza 210 feet wide. Two low earthen burial mounds were once linked to it. The university fully dug one of them in the 1920s. The other, about 60 feet wide and 3 feet tall, sits at the plaza's northern edge. No mounds are known at the other villages.

Newer tools helped finish the count. Using geophysical survey, archaeologists mapped what lay underground without digging. A magnetometer picked up soils changed by houses and trash pits. Electromagnetic induction, which measures how soil carries electricity and responds to magnetism, worked best: the midden stains showed up as bright patches on the maps.

Surveyors had known of four stains before. The new surveys confirmed two more, and a third is suspected, which would bring the total to seven.

## Kentucky today

The site is protected, and its location stays off public maps. Singer-Hieronymus shows that a Scott County farming community stayed in one small area for generations, rebuilding its village again and again instead of moving far away. It is a rare look at how Fort Ancient towns changed over time, and it deserves respect from a distance.

properties.name: Levi Todd / Ellerslie (Lexington co-founder)
properties.title: Levi Todd / Ellerslie (Lexington co-founder)
properties.subtitle: Fayette County · Levi Todd's Ellerslie on Richmond Road · Lexington trustee 1776, county clerk, Blue Licks major · Kentucky career 1775–1807
properties.history:
Levi Todd (1756–1807) came to Kentucky in 1775 with his brothers John and Robert, helped lay out Lexington’s stockade, and was elected one of its first Gentlemen Trustees in March 1776. He became Kentucky County’s first clerk in 1777, rode with George Rogers Clark’s Illinois campaign (including the capture of Kaskaskia in 1778), and later served decades as Fayette County clerk.

In August 1782 he led a forty-man relief column toward Bryan Station, then fought at Blue Licks—where brother Col. John Todd was killed—and wrote one of the earliest official accounts of the defeat. He rose to major general of Kentucky militia, built Ellerslie (Fayette’s first brick house), and was grandfather of Mary Todd Lincoln.

properties.name: New Castle — Henry County seat (1798)
properties.title: New Castle — Henry County seat (1798)
properties.subtitle: Henry County · county cut from Shelby 1798 · courthouse square · incorporated 1817
properties.history:
When the General Assembly cut Henry County from Shelby County in 1798 and named it for Virginia’s Patrick Henry, New Castle was fixed as the seat—just north of Shelby County, inside the Louisville–Lexington–Cincinnati triangle. Landowners opened a courthouse square; the town was incorporated in 1817 and is counted among Kentucky’s oldest incorporated communities. Tobacco, hay, and cattle long carried the surrounding farms, and the courthouse square still anchors a preserved downtown.

The 1863 Caplinger House, built by druggist James N. Caplinger, was the Henry County History Center until it was sold in 2017 and became a private residence.

properties.name: Bryan Station siege (Aug 15–16, 1782)
properties.title: Bryan Station siege (Aug 15–16, 1782)
properties.subtitle: Fayette County · Elkhorn Creek north of Lexington · women at the spring · Caldwell–Girty force
properties.history:
Bryan Station (also Bryan’s / Bryant’s) sat on the south bank of Elkhorn Creek a few miles northeast of Lexington, planted in 1776 by the Bryan brothers and Boone in-laws from North Carolina. On August 15–16, 1782, Capt. William Caldwell, Simon Girty, and several hundred British-allied Wyandot, Lenape, and Shawnee warriors surrounded the fort. Knowing the attackers hoped to ambush men at the spring, the garrison sent the women and girls out with their usual water pails; they filled the fort’s supply and returned unharmed.

The siege failed to take the station; when Kentucky militia pursued three days later, they met disaster at Blue Licks.

properties.name: James Knox / Camp Knox (Skinhouse Branch)
properties.title: James Knox / Camp Knox (Skinhouse Branch)
properties.subtitle: Green County · Skinhouse Branch · long-hunter base camp 1770–71 (an 1892 biography says 1774) · KY Senate 1795–1800
properties.history:
Before Boone’s fame crowded the memory, long hunter Col. James Knox led a party of Virginia and Carolina hunters through Cumberland Gap into Kentucky. The 1942 Historic Camp Knox marker says that in 1770 he settled here with 22 men, who cured and stored 2,300 deer hides and other furs in a skin house; Green County’s history page says the hunters named the branch beside the camp Skinhouse Branch. Kentucky Historical Society marker 709 says Knox led 40 Long Hunters to Kentucky in 1770, built a camp with nine men in what is now Green County, and returned to Virginia in 1771.

Sources differ on dates: an 1892 biography has the party crossing the Gap in 1769 and puts the Green River skin camp in 1774, so this story follows the markers’ 1770–1771. The 1892 biography says the Cherokee leader Captain Dick directed Knox’s men to a stream they named Dick’s (now Dix) River, and another account says Knox named it for him. Knox later recruited a company for Virginia’s 8th Regiment, commanded a company in Morgan’s Rifles at Saratoga (8th Virginia Regiment site), and served in the Kentucky Senate from Lincoln County, 1795–1800 (marker 709).

properties.name: Mammoth Cave saltpeter (War of 1812)
properties.title: Mammoth Cave saltpeter (War of 1812)
properties.subtitle: Edmonson County · Historic Entrance / Rotunda · industrial nitrate mining 1812–1815 · enslaved labor
properties.history: Long before tourism, Mammoth Cave’s nitrate-rich dirt fed gunpowder. In the War of 1812, when British blockade cut imported saltpeter, operators worked the Rotunda and nearby passages at industrial scale—leaching cave soil in wooden vats, pumping liquor to the surface, and converting it to potassium nitrate. Enslaved laborers did most of the hauling and filtering; remnants of vats, pipes, and pump works still stand just inside the Historic Entrance. After the war, when prices fell, the workings were abandoned and the cave became a minor tourist attraction.

properties.name: Harry Innes (Frankfort / federal judge)
properties.title: Harry Innes (Frankfort / federal judge)
properties.subtitle: Franklin County · first U.S. district judge for Kentucky 1789–1816 · statehood conventions · buried Frankfort Cemetery
properties.history:
Virginia lawyer Harry Innes reached Kentucky in 1783 after Virginia elected him an assistant judge of the District of Kentucky’s supreme court; he was sworn in at Crow’s Station, Virginia (near present-day Danville, Kentucky), in November 1782. He served as attorney general for the Kentucky District (1784–1789), sat in eight of the ten statehood conventions that separated Kentucky from Virginia, and on September 26, 1789, became the first U.S. district judge for Kentucky—appointed by George Washington—holding that seat until his death in Frankfort in 1816.

He practiced law, farmed, and speculated in land, served as a Transylvania University trustee, and built a distinguished library; as a federal judge he presided over the first treason trial of Aaron Burr, and he later endured bitter Spanish-conspiracy libel fights with Humphrey Marshall. Frankfort Cemetery holds his grave.

properties.name: Hopkinsville founding (Elizabeth → Hopkinsville)
properties.title: Hopkinsville founding (Elizabeth → Hopkinsville)
properties.subtitle: Christian County seat · Bartholomew Wood donation 1797 · renamed Hopkinsville 1804 for Gen. Samuel Hopkins
properties.history:
Bartholomew Wood claimed a Christian County tract in 1796 and, with his wife Martha Ann, donated five acres and a half interest in Old Rock Spring when the new county seated justice there in 1797. A log courthouse and jail rose by 1798; locals tried the name Elizabeth for the Woods’ eldest daughter, but Elizabethtown already held that name.

In 1804 the General Assembly established the town as Hopkinsville for Gen. Samuel Hopkins—Revolutionary veteran, Transylvania Company agent, and later Henderson County organizer—whose name also marks Hopkins County. It remains Christian County’s seat.

properties.name: Inner Bluegrass phosphatic limestone & horse country
properties.title: Inner Bluegrass phosphatic limestone & horse country
properties.subtitle: Fayette County / Lexington · Lexington–Cynthiana phosphatic limestones · Virginia–Carolina horse settlers ~1780–1820
properties.history:
Inner Bluegrass soils rest on phosphatic Lexington and Cynthiana limestones, with high calcium and phosphorus. University of Kentucky soil tests still show that edge over the rest of the state—about two-thirds of Bluegrass samples testing high for phosphorus in a late twentieth-century lab series.

After the Revolution, from about 1780 to 1820, Virginia and Carolina horse-raising families pushed west onto that forage-rich ground just as industrial America needed more horsepower. UK equine soil scientist Joshua McGrath argues the Horse Capital story starts with geology and settlement timing—high soil phosphorus supporting forage yields before commercial fertilizer—not a magic bone myth alone.

properties.name: McAfee Station on the Salt River
properties.title: McAfee Station on the Salt River
properties.subtitle: Mercer County · McAfee hamlet · McAfee Company survey 1773 · stockade 1779 · New Providence Church 1785
properties.history: In May 1773, Virginia’s McAfee Company—brothers James, Robert, and George, with James McCoun Jr. and Samuel Adams—surveyed fertile Salt River bottomlands in today’s Mercer County. After Point Pleasant service and delayed returns, they built a stockade on James McAfee’s land in 1779; by 1781 nearly every local family sheltered there, and a Shawnee attack that May was beaten back with help from nearby stations. New Providence Presbyterian Church (1785) grew from the same community, and the station area is now part of an unincorporated Mercer County community.

properties.name: Blue Jacket at Limestone (Maysville)
properties.title: Blue Jacket at Limestone (Maysville)
properties.subtitle: Mason County · Limestone landing · Shawnee war chief Weyapiersenwah · 1787 negotiation & 1788 Kentucky raids
properties.history: Shawnee war chief Blue Jacket (c. 1743–1810) first appears in written records at his Scioto town in 1773, fought at Point Pleasant in Lord Dunmore’s War, and allied with the British through the Revolution. Benjamin Logan’s 1786 Kentucky militia expedition burned his Bellefontaine-area town; he negotiated with Kentuckians at Limestone (Maysville) in 1787, then raided back into Kentucky in 1788. With Miami chief Little Turtle he helped shatter Harmar’s and St. Clair’s armies (1790–91)—St. Clair’s Defeat remains the U.S. Army’s worst loss to Native forces—before defeat at Fallen Timbers (1794) and the Treaty of Greenville (1795) that opened much of Ohio to settlement and reshaped the Ohio–Kentucky frontier.

properties.name: Slone Site (15Pi11), Pike County
properties.title: Slone Site (15Pi11), Pike County
properties.subtitle: Pike County · Fort Ancient circular village ~1350–1400 CE
properties.history:
Around 1350 CE, Fort Ancient farmers in Pike County built a round village behind a wooden wall. They lived there for only thirty to forty-five years. The evidence comes from how many times they rebuilt their houses and the wall. In that time, the village grew so much that its wall had to be moved outward twice.

We know so much about Slone because so much of it was dug. In 1963 and 1964, before a reservoir project flooded the area, University of Kentucky crews excavated about eighty percent of the site. That makes it one of the most complete views of a late Middle Fort Ancient village in eastern Kentucky.

The village was laid out in rings. At the center was an open plaza. Around it was a band for cooking and storage, with hearths, earth ovens and storage pits. There was very little trash in this band, so residents probably swept it clean.

Next came the houses, at least twelve of them. On average, each was about 19 by 28 feet, with a hearth in the middle. Behind the houses, families piled their trash: broken jars, broken arrowheads and animal bone. Family cemeteries were also placed behind the homes, keeping relatives close.

A palisade surrounded everything. The first wall made the village just over 200 feet across. Later, residents took that wall down, built new houses where it had stood, and put up a second wall about 240 feet across. Near the end, a third wall reached about 255 feet.

The walls may have protected the village from attack. They also marked clearly who belonged inside.

Slone is also known for its stone discoidals. Crews found more than 150 of these round stones. Most were sandstone, and a few were made of cannel coal, hematite or limestone. Most were plain and smooth on both sides, and a few were polished or decorated with cut lines.

People probably used them to play chunkey. In this game, one player rolled the stone across a flat field and players threw spears or shot arrows after it. Whoever landed closest to where the stone stopped scored a point.

## Kentucky today

The village site now lies under water, and its location is protected on this map. What survives is the record from 1963–64 and the collections it produced. In Pike County, Slone shows that walled farming towns were part of mountain life long before the frontier. Its many game stones show that everyday life there also had room for play.

properties.title: Louisville & Nashville Railroad (main line opens)
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County · Louisville Union Station / 10th & Broadway · charter 1850 · Louisville–Nashville open 1859
properties.history: Kentucky chartered the Louisville & Nashville on March 5, 1850, to build south toward Nashville; Tennessee authorized the extension in 1851. Track laying began in Louisville in May 1853; the first eight-mile excursion ran August 25, 1855, and on October 27, 1859, the first train covered the full ~187-mile Louisville–Nashville main line. properties.name: William Hoy’s Station (Madison County)
properties.title: William Hoy’s Station (Madison County)
properties.subtitle: Madison County · Hoy’s Station (USGS historic locale) · established 1781 · August 1782 captives Jones Hoy & Jack Calloway
properties.history:
William Hoy established Hoy’s Station in Madison County in 1781, with help from George Boone, according to a Boone-family genealogy; a Filson Historical Society study of pioneer forts and stations places it about six miles northwest of present-day Richmond. In 1782, Wyandot warriors captured two boys, Jones Hoy and Jack Calloway, near Boonesborough.

On August 12, 1782, Capt. John Holder and 17 militiamen overtook the band on Great Salt Creek (the Licking River); Holder lost four men in the skirmish and, outnumbered, withdrew without the boys. Jones Hoy was held captive for seven years, Calloway not as long. The Kentucky Historical Society’s Upper Blue Licks marker (Nicholas County) records that skirmish but does not mention the station or say how the boys were tied to it, so the map pin uses the USGS historic-locale point for William Hoy’s Station—an approximate site.

properties.name: Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill
properties.title: Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill
properties.subtitle: Mercer County · Shaker Village of Pleasant Hill (Shakertown) · Shaker mission 1805 · hilltop village 1808 · closed as a religious society by 1910
properties.history:
In 1805 three Shaker missionaries—John Meacham, Issachar Bates and Benjamin Seth Youngs—left New York and traveled mostly on foot to Kentucky, and in August found three Kentuckians willing to listen, who soon became the state’s first Shaker converts. Believers began moving to Elisha Thomas’s 140-acre Mercer County farm; 44 people signed the first family covenant in December 1806, and two years later they moved to a nearby hilltop they named Pleasant Hill.

By 1823 the village had 491 Shakers on about 4,500 acres, and over 105 years they built more than 260 structures, including one of Kentucky’s earliest municipal water systems. By 1816 they were shipping brooms, cooperage, preserves and seeds on trading trips to New Orleans by river. Pleasant Hill closed as an active religious society by 1910 and the last Shaker died in 1923; a nonprofit formed in 1961 has since restored the village.

properties.name: Camp Nelson (Civil War depot and USCT recruiting center)
properties.title: Camp Nelson (Civil War depot and USCT recruiting center)
properties.subtitle: Jessamine County · Camp Nelson National Monument · depot 1863 · USCT recruiting 1864 · Home for Colored Refugees 1865
properties.history:
The U.S. Army established Camp Nelson in central Kentucky in April 1863 as a fortified supply depot, forward base and hospital, part of the Union effort to liberate East Tennessee. At its 1865 height it covered roughly 4,000 acres and more than 300 buildings, with earthen forts built primarily by enslaved African Americans impressed by the Army.

From 1864 thousands of Black men, women and children reached the camp; eight regiments of United States Colored Troops were organized there, making it the largest USCT recruitment center in Kentucky and the third largest in the nation. In November 1864 soldiers expelled more than 400 women and children and destroyed their huts, and more than one hundred of the displaced refugees died of illness and exposure. The Army then built a Home for Colored Refugees, opened in January 1865, and on March 3, 1865 an Act of Congress emancipated the wives, children and mothers of USCT soldiers.

Camp Nelson became a national monument in 2018; the pin marks the monument, not the whole camp.

properties.name: Andalex Village (15Hk22), Hopkins County
properties.title: Andalex Village (15Hk22), Hopkins County
properties.subtitle: Hopkins County · Mississippian mound center · occupation AD 1175–1275 · county-level pin (site location not public)
properties.history:
The Andalex site is in Hopkins County, where Mississippian farmers occupied a mound center from AD 1175 to 1275. Cultural Resource Analysts investigated it in 1988 and 1989, before a coal mine was developed, and documented a platform mound, at least eleven houses around a central plaza, and a palisade enclosing the community. The mound ended up five feet tall and about 75 by 85 feet; it grew in three stages as the leader’s house on top was rebuilt and the mound capped with clay.

Residents made shell-tempered Mississippi Plain jars, some with incised geometric designs on the necks (incised types), hunted mainly deer, grew corn, marshelder, maygrass and lambsquarters, and collected hickory nuts. The state archaeology site does not publish the location, so the pin is a county-level point for Hopkins County.

properties.name: Louisville and Portland Canal (locks)
properties.title: Louisville and Portland Canal (locks)
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County · Louisville and Portland Canal lock site · chartered 1825 · construction 1826 · opened 1830
properties.history:
The Falls of the Ohio form the only barrier to navigation between Pittsburgh and New Orleans, and cargo was portaged around them except for a few weeks of high water each spring. Kentucky chartered the private Louisville and Portland Canal Company in 1825; construction started March 1, 1826, and the canal opened in 1830. As built, it was 1.9 miles long and 64 feet wide and ended in a three-flight lock with a total lift of 26 feet.

It was the first major improvement completed on a major U.S. river and was fully completed in 1833. The route was later enlarged and rebuilt and is now the McAlpine Locks and Dam canal; the pin marks the lock site at the downstream end.
