properties.name: Col. John Hardin’s Pleasant Run homestead (approximate)
properties.title: Col. John Hardin’s Pleasant Run homestead (approximate)
properties.subtitle: Washington County · Pleasant Run, ~3 mi east of Springfield (approximate) · settled April 1786 · killed on 1792 peace mission
properties.history:
John Hardin was born in Virginia in 1753. In August 1774, at the start of Lord Dunmore’s War, he was wounded in a skirmish at Snake’s Town on the Muskingum during Angus McDonald’s expedition; the musket ball lodged in his thigh near the groin and stayed there for the rest of his life.

In the Revolution he was a lieutenant picked for Daniel Morgan’s riflemen and fought at Saratoga under Morgan. In April 1786 he settled his family on Pleasant Run, a branch of Beech Fork, about three miles east of present-day Springfield in what is now Washington County, Kentucky; the family farmed, raised livestock and joined the Methodist church. As a militia captain that year he attacked a Piankashaw village near Vincennes, although the Piankashaw were friendly to the Americans.

Promoted to colonel, he led the Kentucky militia detachment routed in 1790 at Heller’s Corner—“Hardin’s Defeat”—which began a long run of American losses to the Miami chief Little Turtle, and in 1791 he led mounted militia against a Kickapoo village during Gen. Charles Scott’s Wabash campaign. In May 1792 Gen. James Wilkinson sent him to carry American peace terms to the nations along the Sandusky River. A Shawnee party offered to escort him, then killed him and his servant Freeman one night as he slept.

Hardin County, Kentucky, and the town of Hardin, Ohio, near where he was killed, are named for him. His son Martin D. Hardin, later a U.S. senator from Kentucky, married Ann Logan, daughter of Gen. Benjamin Logan. The map pin is an approximate point about three miles east of Springfield, where the Kentucky Historical Society’s John Hardin marker stands on US 150 and where his son Mark Hardin placed the homestead; the exact house site is not mapped.

properties.name: Carrollton (Port William) at the Kentucky–Ohio confluence
properties.title: Carrollton (Port William) at the Kentucky–Ohio confluence
properties.subtitle: Carroll County · Point Park at the mouth of the Kentucky River · settled 1792 · incorporated as Port William 1794 · Gallatin County seat · renamed Carrollton 1838
properties.history:
Where the Kentucky River empties into the Ohio, Gen. Charles Scott built a blockhouse in 1789 to protect settlers, according to the Kentucky Historical Society marker at Point Park. The town at the river mouth was first settled in 1792 and called Port William. Benjamin Craig, who had come to Kentucky with the Traveling Church led by his brother Lewis Craig, laid off the town on 613 acres that he and James Hawkins owned, and the legislature incorporated Port William in 1794; Craig had built the first brick house in the county in 1792.

When Gallatin County was formed on December 14, 1798, from parts of Franklin and Shelby counties, Port William served as its county seat. The first Gallatin County court met on May 14, 1799, at the brick home of Richard and Sarah Masterson—leading Methodists, and Richard an early trustee of Port William—which still stands on the east side of town.

In 1838 the Kentucky legislature formed Carroll County, partly out of Gallatin, and changed the town’s name to Carrollton, both in honor of Charles Carroll of Carrollton, the Maryland signer of the Declaration of Independence; Carrollton became the new county’s seat. The map pin marks Point Park at the confluence.

properties.name: Rowlandton Mound Site (15McN3), McCracken County
properties.title: Rowlandton Mound Site (15McN3), McCracken County
properties.subtitle: McCracken County · Mississippian platform mound and village · occupation ~1100–1350 CE · pin generalized
properties.history:
Around 1100 CE, people in McCracken County began building a town around a large earthen mound. For about 250 years, until roughly 1350, the Rowlandton Mound Site was a home and a civic center. It covered about three hectares, or seven and a half acres. That is roughly the size of Wickliffe Mounds, the best-known Mississippian town in far western Kentucky.

The town was part of the Mississippian world. Across the Southeast and the Midwest, corn-farming communities built platform mounds: flat-topped earthen mounds that raised important buildings above everyone else. Rowlandton had one large platform mound with a village beside it. Building a mound like this took organized work over many seasons.

That suggests leaders who could gather their neighbors to help, and a town that wanted to be seen.

For years, archaeologists had a ready explanation for towns like this. Western Kentucky civic centers such as Rowlandton, the Twin Mounds site and the Tolu site were thought to be thirteenth-century outposts of Kincaid Mounds, a powerful center across the Ohio in southern Illinois. Excavations in 2006 by Kit Wesler of Murray State University showed that this was not the case. Instead, these centers were probably started by local Late Woodland people, whose families had lived in the area for generations before Mississippian ways took hold.

That changes how we picture western Kentucky at the time. These weren't colonies set up by outsiders. Local communities adopted new ideas about farming, building and leadership, and changed their own landscape to match. Like many Mississippian towns in the region, Rowlandton was left behind by the mid-1300s. That was a time when people across the lower Ohio Valley were reorganizing and moving.

## Kentucky today

The site is protected, and its map pin is generalized to guard against looting. Rowlandton shows that McCracken County was home to a planned Mississippian town built by people with deep local roots, long before the river trade that later shaped the county. The best way to honor it is to learn about it from a distance.

David Pollack's account of the site is in The Archaeology of Kentucky: An Update, published by the Kentucky Heritage Council in 2008.

properties.name: Hidden River Cave (Horse Cave)
properties.title: Hidden River Cave (Horse Cave)
properties.subtitle: Hart County · sinkhole entrance at 119 E. Main St., Horse Cave · turbine 1890 · generator 1892 · tours 1912–1943 · American Cave Museum 1992
properties.history:
Hidden River Cave lies directly beneath the town of Horse Cave in Hart County, and its main entrance is a large sinkhole at 119 East Main Street. The cave stream was the town’s water source, and attempts to set up public waterworks in the cave go back to 1879. Dentist George A. Thomas moved to Horse Cave in 1888, bought a house by the entrance and, a year later, bought the cave for $375.

In 1890 a vertical-shaft turbine was built below the junction of the two cave streams to drive the pumps, and in 1892 an added electrical generator lit the Thomas home, his dental office and two other buildings—making Horse Cave, the cave’s operators say, the first town in Kentucky with incandescent lights (Louisville had electric arc lights earlier). The cave offered commercial tours from 1912 through 1943, though the same history dates the opening of a half-mile tour section to 1916.

Domestic and industrial sewage dumped into sinkholes and wells fouled the stream; with noxious odors, low wartime visitation and a failed lawsuit, the tours closed in 1943, and the cave became known as one of the most polluted in America. A regional sewage treatment system stopped the sewage in December 1989, the stream began to recover, and in 1992 the American Cave Museum opened beside the entrance and the steps down to the underground river were rebuilt. Tours reached Sunset Dome again in 2020.

properties.name: Canewood, Gen. Charles Scott’s last home (KHS marker #116)
properties.title: Canewood, Gen. Charles Scott’s last home (KHS marker #116)
properties.subtitle: Clark County · KHS marker #116, KY 627 about 6½ mi N of Winchester · Scott in Kentucky 1785–1813 · Scott’s Landing/Petersburg near Versailles not mapped
properties.history:
Revolutionary War general Charles Scott first saw Kentucky in 1785, coming down the Ohio to Limestone, and moved his family out in 1787 to land near present-day Versailles, where he built a two-story log house, a stockade, and a tobacco inspection warehouse at what became Scott's Landing. That June, Shawnee warriors killed his son Samuel as he crossed the Ohio in a canoe while Scott watched from the bank, and another son, Merritt, was killed in Harmar's 1790 campaign. Scott sold lots for a town he called Petersburg and offered it as the new state capital in 1792, but Frankfort won, and Petersburg never grew into a real town.

In 1791 he led Kentucky mounted volunteers against the Wea towns on the Wabash. He went on to lead Kentucky's mounted volunteers under Anthony Wayne at Fallen Timbers in 1794, served as the fourth governor from 1808 to 1812, died at his Canewood estate in 1813, and was reburied in Frankfort Cemetery in 1854. Scott County and Scottsville are named for him.

The map pin marks the Kentucky Historical Society's Canewood marker in Clark County, for the house Scott shared with his wife, the widow of Col. Nathaniel Gist, in his last years; the sites of Scott's Landing and Petersburg near Versailles are not mapped.

properties.name: Flemingsburg (Fleming County courthouse)
properties.title: Flemingsburg (Fleming County courthouse)
properties.subtitle: Fleming County · courthouse lawn, Flemingsburg (KHS marker #950) · Stockton’s Station 1787 · Fleming’s Station 1788 · county seat 1798 · incorporated 1812
properties.history:
Col. John Fleming came into the hill country south of Limestone in 1776 to mark and improve land, served as an officer in the Revolution, and built Fleming's Station in 1788. It was the second fort in the area. The first was Stockton's Station, built in 1787 by his half-brother, Maj. George Stockton, who had raised a crop on the spot in 1786 while still living at Strode's Station.

Stockton owned the land where the town grew, laid it out in the mid-1790s (the Kentucky Historical Society marker says 1796), and named it for his half-brother. When Fleming County was cut from Mason in 1798 as Kentucky's 26th county, Flemingsburg became its seat, and the legislature incorporated the town in 1812. The country stayed dangerous for years: Robert Stockton was killed by Indians in 1789 and still lies under stacked rock slabs in a field in eastern Fleming County. The map pin marks the Fleming County marker on the courthouse lawn in Flemingsburg.

properties.name: Stitzel Brothers Distillery remains, 25th & Maple, Louisville
properties.title: Stitzel Brothers Distillery remains, 25th & Maple, Louisville
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County · 2501 Maple St., western Louisville · Stitzel barrel-rack patent 1879 · Stitzel-Weller opens in Shively 1935
properties.history:
Before 1879, Kentucky warehousemen rolled barrels into lines on the floor, laid a pair of wooden rails across them, and rolled another row on top, three or four barrels high. Reaching a bottom barrel meant taking the whole line apart, the weight made the lower barrels leak, and poor air flow could leave whiskey musty after a hot summer. Louisville distiller Frederick Stitzel, working on the problem at the Glencoe Distillery, patented a fix in 1879: timber frames with projecting rails, so every barrel rested on its own ledge with air all around it and any one could be rolled out without disturbing the rest.

The racks stood free of the building's walls, and insurance maps of the era started labeling such buildings "patent warehouses." The rick system is still the standard in Kentucky rickhouses, and the family name carried on: the A. Ph. Stitzel Distillery later joined W. L. Weller & Sons, and Stitzel-Weller opened in Shively on Derby Day 1935.

Stitzel’s racks came eighteen years before E. H. Taylor Jr.’s Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897. The map pin marks the surviving buildings of the Stitzel Brothers Distillery at 25th and Maple streets in western Louisville; the site of the Glencoe Distillery is not mapped.

properties.name: Jeptha’s Knob marker, Clay Village (KHS #161)
properties.title: Jeptha’s Knob marker, Clay Village (KHS #161)
properties.subtitle: Shelby County · KHS marker #161 at Clay Village @ Jeptha Knob Road · suspected impact structure · described 1887 (Linney), mapped 1925 (Bucher) · knob on private land
properties.history:
About eight miles east of Shelbyville near Clay Village, Jeptha Knob rises some 300 feet above the surrounding farmland and is the highest point in the Bluegrass. Underneath is a circular structure nearly three miles across: a core of uplifted, shattered Ordovician limestone and shale ringed by concentric and radial faults, later buried under flat-lying Silurian rock. William Linney of the Kentucky Geological Survey first described it in 1887, and Walter Bucher mapped it in 1925 and called it "cryptovolcanic," the word still on its roadside marker.

Most geologists now suspect a meteorite or comet strike around the end of the Ordovician, roughly 440 million years ago, and unusually high iridium in its broken rock points that way, but it isn't on the official list of impact craters because no shatter cones or coesite have been found. The knob is on private land. The years on this story are the human ones, from Linney’s 1887 report to Bucher’s 1925 map.

The map pin marks the Kentucky Historical Society’s Jeptha’s Knob marker at Clay Village; the knob itself is private.

properties.name: Daniel Trabue House, Columbia (KHS marker #1782)
properties.title: Daniel Trabue House, Columbia (KHS marker #1782)
properties.subtitle: Adair County · 299 Jamestown St., Columbia · KHS marker #1782 · house built ca. 1823 · Trabue in Kentucky 1778–1840
properties.history:
Daniel Trabue (1760–1840), raised in Chesterfield County, Virginia, and descended from French Huguenots, came through Cumberland Gap as a teenager with his brother James and spent nearly three years in Kentucky, at Fort Boonesborough and Logan’s Fort. He went back to Virginia, peddled goods to American soldiers during the Yorktown campaign, married Mary Haskins in 1782, and brought his family down the Ohio in 1785.

After several years in Fayette County near the Kentucky River, the family moved to the Green River country in present Adair County. There Trabue helped survey and establish the town of Columbia and served as town trustee, sheriff, and justice of the peace while running a grist mill, an inn, and a store.

About 1823 he built a brick house on a hill above town; money troubles forced the family out in 1828. In 1827 he wrote his memoir of the pioneer years, including events at Logan’s Station, Boonesborough, and service under Anthony Wayne. It survives in the Draper Manuscripts and is read today as Westward into Kentucky: The Narrative of Daniel Trabue.

The map pin marks his house at 299 Jamestown Street in Columbia (KHS marker #1782).

properties.name: Russellville (Logan Court House), Logan County courthouse square
properties.title: Russellville (Logan Court House), Logan County courthouse square
properties.subtitle: Logan County · downtown Russellville at the courthouse square · Cook’s Station 1790 · Logan Court House 1792 · named for Gen. William Russell 1798 · established 1810
properties.history:
The Logan County seat started as a spring with a string of names: Big Boiling Spring, Gasper Butcher’s Spring, Butcher’s Station. A local historian put Butcher there around 1780, but others have questioned it, and historian W. R. Jillson found no written record of anyone living on the site before 1790, when William Cook and his wife built Cook’s Cabin (Cook’s Station) about a mile east of today’s town, joined by 18-year-old William Stewart. The settlement became Logan Court House when it was picked as the seat of the new Logan County in 1792.

Gen. William Russell, who held a 2,000-acre grant there for Revolutionary War service, donated land for the platted county seat in 1795; the town took his name in 1798, and the legislature formally established it on Jan. 15, 1810. The same county saw the Rev. James McGready’s June 1800 camp meeting at the Red River Meeting House, often counted as the start of the Revival of 1800, and Andrew Jackson’s fatal 1806 duel with Charles Dickinson at Harrison’s Mill. The map pin marks downtown Russellville at the courthouse square.
properties.description:
The Logan County seat started as a spring with a string of names: Big Boiling Spring, Gasper Butcher’s Spring, Butcher’s Station. A local historian put Butcher there around 1780, but others have questioned it, and historian W. R. Jillson found no written record of anyone living on the site before 1790, when William Cook and his wife built Cook’s Cabin (Cook’s Station) about a mile east of today’s town, joined by 18-year-old William Stewart. The settlement became Logan Court House when it was picked as the seat of the new Logan County in 1792.

Gen. William Russell, who held a 2,000-acre grant there for Revolutionary War service, donated land for the platted county seat in 1795; the town took his name in 1798, and the legislature formally established it on Jan. 15, 1810. The same county saw the Rev. James McGready’s June 1800 camp meeting at the Red River Meeting House, often counted as the start of the Revival of 1800, and Andrew Jackson’s fatal 1806 duel with Charles Dickinson at Harrison’s Mill. The map pin marks downtown Russellville at the courthouse square.

properties.name: Pilot Knob State Nature Preserve (Boone’s Overlook)
properties.title: Pilot Knob State Nature Preserve (Boone’s Overlook)
properties.subtitle: Powell County · Pilot Knob State Nature Preserve · Boone and Finley’s traditional first view of the Bluegrass, June 7, 1769 · preserve dedicated 1985
properties.history:
Pilot Knob, a 730-foot sandstone outcrop in Powell County, is believed to be where Daniel Boone and John Finley first looked out over the Bluegrass. By tradition they reached the summit on June 7, 1769, before making camp and exploring the country beyond; Finley called it “the beautiful level of Kentucky,” and John Filson’s 1784 Boone narrative has Boone recalling that he “had gained the summit of a commanding ridge” and “beheld the ample plains, the beauteous tracts below.” The Kentucky Historical Society marks June 7 as Boone Day.

The knob, also called Boone’s Overlook, is Pennsylvanian conglomerate sandstone, and pieces of it were once quarried for millstones. From the top you can see the Cumberland Plateau, the Knobs, and the Bluegrass. The state dedicated the first 308 acres as Pilot Knob State Nature Preserve on Sept. 26, 1985; it has since grown to about 1,258 acres with two strenuous trails. The map pin marks the preserve, near the knob.

properties.name: Red Bird Petroglyphs (15CY51)
properties.title: Red Bird Petroglyphs (15CY51)
properties.subtitle: Clay County (generalized) · carvings undated · fell Dec. 7, 1994; now in Rawlings–Stinson Park, Clay County
properties.history:
A 50-ton sandstone block cut with petroglyphs sat in Clay County. The inscribed face was about 5½ feet high and 20 feet long, with sharp, linear carvings that the authors of Rock Art of Kentucky called “different from any of the previously reported Kentucky petroglyphs.” Nobody has dated them: a state marker credits a legendary Cherokee chief named Red Bird, but the Kentucky Historical Society itself has said there are no reliable dates, and writers have described the marks as possibly Native, colonial, or both.

That gap is why this story carries no years. The site, 15CY51, went on the National Register in September 1989. Construction work undercut the face, and on Dec. 7, 1994, the block fell; two days later it was moved to Rawlings–Stinson Park in Clay County, where it sits roofed and fenced.

It was taken off the Register in 2003. A sign at the park claims eight Old World alphabets on the stone, a fringe claim scholars reject. The map pin is generalized.

properties.name: McLean Drift Bank, old Paradise on the Green River (generalized)
properties.title: McLean Drift Bank, old Paradise on the Green River (generalized)
properties.subtitle: Muhlenberg County · Green River at the lost town of Paradise (generalized point) · first commercial coal mine in Kentucky 1820 · TVA buyout of Paradise 1967
properties.history:
Explorer Thomas Walker found coal in what would become Kentucky in 1750 and burned it in his campfire, but nobody mined it for sale for another seventy years. In 1820 Kentucky’s first commercial coal mine, the McLean Drift Bank, opened along the Green River at what became the village of Paradise in Muhlenberg County, and it produced 328 tons in its first year. For decades the Western Coalfield carried the whole state: 100,000 tons by 1843 and a million tons by 1879, the year the first commercial mine in the Eastern Coalfield opened in Bell County.

Paradise began as Stom’s Landing, named for Leonard Stom, who ran a ferry there, and it became a coal-mining town. The sources don’t say when the drift bank itself closed. TVA began building its Paradise coal plant on the town site in 1959, bought out the last residents in 1967, and demolished the town, which lives on in John Prine’s song “Paradise.”

The exact mine site isn’t published, so the map pin is a generalized point at old Paradise.

properties.name: Gen. James Wilkinson’s Love House site, Frankfort (KHS marker #1182)
properties.title: Gen. James Wilkinson’s Love House site, Frankfort (KHS marker #1182)
properties.subtitle: Franklin County · Wapping & Wilkinson Sts., Frankfort · house built ca. 1786 by Wilkinson · Frankfort laid out 1786 · Spanish oath 1787 · Frankfort land sold 1792
properties.history:
James Wilkinson (1757–1825), born in Maryland, was brevetted a brigadier general in November 1777, at 20, after carrying news of the Saratoga victory to Congress, though he was soon pushed to resign. He moved to Kentucky in 1784 and threw himself into the fight to separate from Virginia. He bought land at Frank’s Ford on the Kentucky River from Humphrey Marshall, won Virginia’s approval in 1786 to lay out a town there, and drew the street plan of what became Frankfort; about 1786 he also built the house later called the Love House, where the legislature first met in 1793.

In April 1787 he made a trading trip down the Mississippi to New Orleans, capital of Spanish Louisiana, where Gov. Esteban Miró agreed to let Kentucky trade on the river in return for Wilkinson’s promise to serve Spanish interests. On Aug. 22, 1787, Wilkinson signed an expatriation declaration and swore allegiance to the King of Spain. His “First Memorial” urged Spain to take Kentuckians under its protection, and his letters were written in a cipher called “Number 13,” the source of his nickname, Agent 13.

He chaired a committee at the November 1788 separation convention but could not swing it toward Spain, and in 1792 he sold his Frankfort land to Andrew Holmes. He went on to serve twice as the senior officer of the U.S. Army while still secretly taking Spanish money. Historian Charles Gayarré published his letters to Miró in 1854, proving what many had suspected.

Theodore Roosevelt wrote that “in all our history, there is no more despicable character,” and Frederick Jackson Turner called him “the most consummate artist in treason that the nation ever possessed.” The map pin marks the site of the Love House at Wapping and Wilkinson streets in Frankfort (KHS marker #1182).

properties.name: Hodgenville (Hodgen’s Mill), KHS marker #1096
properties.title: Hodgenville (Hodgen’s Mill), KHS marker #1096
properties.subtitle: LaRue County · Hodgenville, KY 61 · Phillips Fort 1780 · Hodgen’s mill 1789 · town established Feb. 1818 · LaRue County seat 1843
properties.history:
The LaRue County seat grew up around a gristmill. The county’s first settlement was Phillips Fort, built in 1780 on the North Fork of the Nolin River by surveyor Philip Phillips and a company of settlers from Pennsylvania; it served as a refuge from Indian raids until about 1786, when it was safe enough to build homes, and it was then abandoned and taken down. Robert Hodgen, a Pennsylvania-born tavern keeper who bought land in the area, built a gristmill on the Nolin in 1789 within the protection of the fort.

After his death, his widow and children petitioned for a town, and in February 1818 the Hardin County Court established Hodgenville on 27 acres of Hodgen land. The post office opened in 1826 (spelled Hodgensville until 1904), the town incorporated in 1839, and when LaRue County was formed from Hardin County on March 1, 1843, Hodgenville became its seat.

In between, on Feb. 12, 1809, Abraham Lincoln was born in a cabin on Sinking Spring Farm a few miles south. For the centennial of his birth, Adolph Weinman’s bronze seated Lincoln was dedicated on the town square on May 31, 1909, with Robert Todd Lincoln in the crowd of more than 10,000. The map pin marks the KHS Hodgenville marker (#1096) in town.

properties.name: Warriors’ Path (Athiamiowee), KHS marker #697, Gray Hawk
properties.title: Warriors’ Path (Athiamiowee), KHS marker #697, Gray Hawk
properties.subtitle: Jackson County · US 421 at Gray Hawk; the path ran along War Fork two miles east · Shawnee–Cherokee trail · travelers 1674–1769
properties.history:
Long before the Wilderness Road, the main north–south route through eastern Kentucky was a Native trail the Shawnee called Athiamiowee, the “Path of the Armed Ones.” It linked the Shawnee and other nations north of the Ohio with the Cherokee towns of east Tennessee and the southern Appalachians. Like most Native routes it followed old game trails worn by elk and buffalo through gaps and valleys, and it was marked or blazed along the way.

The Shawnee and Cherokee, often bitter enemies, both used it to reach the Kentucky hunting grounds and to raid each other, and English speakers were calling it the Warriors’ Path by the 1750s. In Kentucky it came north through Cumberland Gap, crossed the Cumberland River at Cumberland Ford (present Pineville), followed the river toward Flat Lick, then ran overland to Goose Creek in Clay County and along War Fork in Jackson County. It crossed Powell County and part of Clark County near the Shawnee town of Eskippakithiki, crossed the Licking River near Blue Licks, and reached the Ohio at Cabin Creek in Mason County.

Gabriel Arthur followed it in 1674 after his Native captors released him, and Thomas Walker in 1750, Christopher Gist in 1751, and John Finley with Daniel Boone in 1769 all used it; John Filson’s 1784 map of Kentucky shows it. A Kentucky Historical Society marker (#697) on US 421 at Gray Hawk notes that the path ran along War Fork two miles east, and the map pin marks that marker.

properties.name: Old Fort Earthworks (15Gp1), Greenup County (generalized)
properties.title: Old Fort Earthworks (15Gp1), Greenup County (generalized)
properties.subtitle: Greenup County (generalized point) · Middle Woodland square enclosure, about 200 BC–AD 500
properties.history:
In Greenup County, Middle Woodland builders (about 200 BC to AD 500) raised part of a much larger Hopewell ceremonial complex. Old Fort Earthworks (site 15Gp1) is a square earthen enclosure on a broad terrace. It surrounds 13.5 acres; its north and south walls run 825 feet and its east and west walls 822 feet, and its corners, not its walls, point to the four cardinal directions.

Pairs of long, low parallel embankments, the “arms,” run out from the east and west walls, and walled roads once tied this enclosure to the rest of the complex, which E. G. Squier mapped in 1847. In 1774 a surveying party under Hanson, laying off land for Patrick Henry, noted the enclosure in their journal and wrongly guessed it was the ruin of a 1750s stone trading house. WPA crews mapped and trenched it in 1938, the only systematic excavation, and found how the walls were built: the builders left the old topsoil in place, spread about two feet of nearby soil and humus over it, heaped thousands of basketloads of sand, gravel, loam, and clay into a six-foot core, then dressed the slope with yellow-brown clay.

They also filled ravines and cut slopes to keep the walls level, and they and later Native groups kept the interior clean. It was listed on the National Register on Dec. 4, 1980. The official Register title is in the research notes. The Kentucky Archaeological Survey does not publish site locations, so the map pin is generalized to protect the site.

properties.name: Cane Ridge Meeting House (KHS marker #51)
properties.title: Cane Ridge Meeting House (KHS marker #51)
properties.subtitle: Bourbon County · Cane Ridge, about 6 mi. east of Paris · log meeting house 1791 · camp meeting Aug. 1801 · Springfield Presbytery dissolved 1804
properties.history:
About six miles east of Paris in Bourbon County, Presbyterian settlers built a meeting house of blue ash logs in 1791 on a ridge named for its canebrakes. Enslaved worshippers sat in a gallery reached by an outside ladder at the west end until an 1829 renovation removed it. Barton W. Stone began preaching at Cane Ridge in 1796.

In August 1801 the congregation invited neighboring Presbyterian and Methodist churches to its annual communion, and from Aug. 6 to Aug. 12 or 13 the crowds kept coming. Estimates run from 10,000 to 20,000 or more; The Encyclopedia of the Stone-Campbell Movement figures that 20,000 could have come at some point during the week, nearly a tenth of Kentucky’s 1800 population, though probably no more than 10,000 at once. Eighteen Presbyterian ministers and numerous Methodists and Baptists preached, often at the same time in different parts of the camp, from the meeting house, outdoor platforms, stumps, wagons, and fallen trees, and 800 to 1,100 people took communion.

It was the largest and most famous camp meeting of the Second Great Awakening and set off a wave of smaller camp meetings across the frontier. In 1804 Stone and other Presbyterian ministers signed “The Last Will and Testament of the Springfield Presbytery” at Cane Ridge (the state marker dates the new “Christian Church” to June 28, 1804), starting a movement that joined Thomas and Alexander Campbell’s followers in 1832.

In the 1930s a stone building was put up around the original log meeting house, which still stands inside it. The map pin marks the meeting house.

properties.name: John Bradford’s Fairfield, KHS marker #1864 (Kentucky Gazette printer)
properties.title: John Bradford’s Fairfield, KHS marker #1864 (Kentucky Gazette printer)
properties.subtitle: Fayette County · 1916 Iron Works Pike, north of Lexington · Kentucke Gazette first printed Aug. 11, 1787 · Transylvania board chair 1793–1830
properties.history:
John Bradford (1749–1830), born in Prince William County, Virginia, first came to Kentucky with a surveying party in 1775 and moved his family out in 1784 or 1785. He had little experience as a printer or editor, but with Fielding Bradford he started Kentucky’s first newspaper in Lexington, the Kentucke Gazette. The first issue was printed on Aug. 11, 1787, and the paper switched to the modern spelling of the state’s name in 1789.

It had no rival within 500 miles until 1795. After statehood, Bradford printed the first book published in Kentucky, a compilation of the acts of the legislature’s first session in 1792. He served as a Lexington town trustee, in the legislature, and as Fayette County sheriff, and he helped found Transylvania University, chairing its board of trustees from 1793 until his death in 1830.

Beginning in August 1828 he wrote a series of 66 newspaper articles on Kentucky’s early years: the Indian wars, the fight for free use of the Mississippi and the port of New Orleans, and the ten conventions that led to statehood. Those “Notes” are still a valued source on the era.

On his farm north of Lexington he built a Flemish-bond brick house called Fairfield, about 1785–1800. The map pin marks the Kentucky Historical Society’s John Bradford marker (#1864) at 1916 Iron Works Pike.

properties.name: Carlisle courthouse square (Nicholas County seat since 1816)
properties.title: Carlisle courthouse square (Nicholas County seat since 1816)
properties.subtitle: Nicholas County · Main St., Carlisle · county formed 1799 · seat at Ellisville 1805 · Kincart’s 50-acre gift and new seat 1816
properties.history:
Nicholas County was formed in 1799 from parts of Mason and Bourbon counties and named for Col. George Nicholas, a Revolutionary War veteran who became a popular lawyer in early Kentucky. Its county court first met in 1800 at the home of Martin Baker Jr. at Lower Blue Licks, then in a new courthouse at Blue Licks.

In 1805 the seat moved to a new town, Ellisville, laid out on James Ellis’s farm along the Lexington–Maysville road, where the county’s courthouse stood until 1816. That year the seat moved again. John Kincart, born in 1791 in what became Nicholas County, had inherited his father Samuel’s 200-acre farm in 1813, and in 1816 he gave 50 acres, including the family’s peach orchard, for a new town named Carlisle.

Streets and lots were laid off around the center of the tract, and Kincart took town lots as payment for his land. The present Nicholas County Courthouse is the third on that site, and a monument to Samuel Kincart stands on its north side. Daniel Boone had lived in the county from 1795 to 1799, and his restored cabin in Carlisle is kept by the Carlisle Tourism Commission. The map pin marks the courthouse square.

properties.title: Kentucky Association race course site, E. Fifth & Race Sts., Lexington
properties.subtitle: Fayette County · East End, Lexington · Association formed July 23, 1826 · track land bought 1828–1834 · Phoenix Hotel Handicap 1831 · closed 1933
properties.history:
On July 23, 1826, Bluegrass horsemen formed the Kentucky Association to promote the breeding and racing of Thoroughbreds. Its founders included Henry Clay, Jesse Bledsoe, Dr. Elisha Warfield, and Thomas F. properties.name: Mantle Rock, Trail of Tears campsite (KHS marker #1675)
properties.title: Mantle Rock, Trail of Tears campsite (KHS marker #1675)
properties.subtitle: Livingston County · KY 133, about 3 mi. west of Joy; the arch is ½ mile from the marker · Cherokee detachments camped here winter 1838–39
properties.history:
West of the crossroads of Joy in Livingston County, off KY 133, a sandstone arch about 30 feet high and 188 feet long stands in the woods of the McGilligan Creek watershed, one of the longest natural arches in Kentucky. Nearby runs a stretch of the old Salem–Golconda Road, and in the winter of 1838–39 that road carried the Cherokee Nation’s forced removal on the northern route of the Trail of Tears. Eleven detachments, more than 10,000 Cherokee in all, came this way toward Berry’s Ferry on the Ohio and the crossing to Golconda, Illinois, not yet halfway to Indian Territory.

Ice closed the river that winter. The Peter Hildebrand detachment, about 1,766 people, spent roughly two bitterly cold weeks in camps strung for miles along the road, waiting for the river to thaw enough for the ferry. A state historical marker says the Cherokee sheltered beneath the arch and that many died there; the National Park Service says there were far too many people to camp under it, that historical descriptions point to a long camp along the road, and that there is no evidence of burials at Mantle Rock.

Across the river, many were trapped again between the frozen Ohio and Mississippi, and the detachments reached Oklahoma hundreds fewer than they started. The Nature Conservancy owns the 367-acre preserve. It was listed on the National Register in 2004 as the Mantle Rock Archeological District and certified that year as a site on the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail, and a 2.75-mile loop trail follows about a mile of the old road.

The map pin marks the Kentucky Historical Society’s Mantle Rock marker (#1675) on KY 133.

properties.name: Pound Gap, Pine Mountain (Kentucky side, near Jenkins)
properties.title: Pound Gap, Pine Mountain (Kentucky side, near Jenkins)
properties.subtitle: Letcher County · US 23 at the Virginia line, Jenkins · Ohio Company surveyors 1750, Gist 1751 · Boone and Stoner 1774 · settler families c. 1798 · Civil War 1862, 1864
properties.history:
Pine Mountain is a single ridge of the Appalachians running about 125 miles from near Pioneer, Tennessee, to near Elkhorn City, Kentucky. Its highest point, Birch Knob, rises 3,273 feet on the Kentucky–Virginia border. It has long been a barrier to travel: only two waterways pass through the whole ridge, the Cumberland River at Pineville and the Clear Fork near Jellico, Tennessee.

Travelers crossed at gaps instead, and the best known on the Virginia line is Pound Gap, between Jenkins, Kentucky, and Pound, Virginia. Ohio Company surveyors, possibly including Christopher Gist, passed through it in 1750, and the Kentucky Historical Society’s marker credits Gist with finding the route on April 1, 1751. Hunters used the gap over the following decade.

In 1774 Daniel Boone, who called it “Sounding Gap,” crossed here with Michael Stoner to warn surveyors of a possible Shawnee attack. Around 1798 seven families, the Adamses, Webbs, Caudills, Crafts, Hammonds, Sturgills, and Collinses, came through to settle what became Letcher County, and in 1834 the General Assembly acted to improve the road from Mount Sterling to Pound Gap, a route used to drive horses, hogs, and cattle to Virginia and southern markets. War came through too.

On March 16, 1862, Union troops under Brig. Gen. James A. Garfield forced about 500 Confederates from the gap, and on June 1, 1864, on their last raid into Kentucky, Morgan’s Raiders dislodged Union forces here. U.S. 23 now runs through a cut at the top.

The map pin is an approximate point on the Kentucky side of the gap, near Jenkins.

properties.name: Old Mulkey Meetinghouse State Historic Site, Tompkinsville
properties.title: Old Mulkey Meetinghouse State Historic Site, Tompkinsville
properties.subtitle: Monroe County · KY 1446 south of Tompkinsville · Mill Creek Baptist Church meetinghouse built 1804 · services until 1856 · state park 1931
properties.history:
South of Tompkinsville in Monroe County, off KY 1446, stands a log meetinghouse built in 1804 for the Mill Creek Baptist Church, a congregation of pioneer Baptists from the Carolinas led by John and Philip Mulkey. A religious revival swept Kentucky in the early 1800s, and by 1803 the congregation had grown to 125 members.

The church minutes of May 11, 1804, called for a meetinghouse 50 feet long and 30 feet wide, with jointed wood shingles, five windows, and three doors, its builder to be paid in trade by subscription. The finished building, of half-hewn logs chinked with rocks and mud, is shaped like a cross with twelve corners, said to stand for the twelve apostles or the twelve tribes of Israel, and its three doors are said to symbolize the Trinity. It had no fireplace.

Worshippers warmed their feet in bags of heated stones, and the men took turns tending an outdoor fire and keeping guard. John Mulkey is said to have preached more than 10,000 sermons, and his descendants helped establish more than 50 Disciples of Christ congregations. Services were held there until 1856.

The cemetery holds Revolutionary War soldiers and pioneers, among them Daniel Boone’s sister Hannah Boone Stewart Pennington, who died in 1828. The site became Kentucky’s 19th state park in 1931. It is often called the oldest log meetinghouse in Kentucky, though the state’s nature preserves office calls it the second-oldest church meetinghouse. The map pin marks the meetinghouse.

properties.name: Liberty Hall, 218 Wilkinson St., Frankfort (John Brown house)
properties.title: Liberty Hall, 218 Wilkinson St., Frankfort (John Brown house)
properties.subtitle: Franklin County · Wilkinson & W. Main Sts., Frankfort · lot bought 1796 · house built 1796–1800 · National Historic Landmark 1971
properties.history:
In 1786 James Wilkinson bought much of the land that is now downtown Frankfort and laid out the town, naming its streets for friends, famous people and places, and himself. Three of his streets, Wilkinson, Wapping, and Montgomery (now Main), bound three sides of the Liberty Hall grounds.

In 1796 John Brown (1757–1837) bought the four-acre lot overlooking the Kentucky River. Brown had represented Virginia in the Continental Congress and in the U.S. Congress, where he introduced the bill granting Kentucky statehood, and Kentucky’s legislature then elected him to the U.S. Senate, where he served until 1805. Often away on government business in Philadelphia, he built a two-story, five-bay brick house, one of the earliest brick homes in Frankfort, from bricks fired from clay dug out of its own cellar.

It was substantially complete in 1800, and its glass windows were added in 1804. The National Park Service calls it one of the most perfect examples of Federal domestic architecture ever realized in the country, patterned on the finest houses Brown had seen in the East. The grounds also held a kitchen and laundry, a smokehouse, a privy, stables, a carriage house, and slave quarters.

In 1835 Brown divided the property so his sons would inherit equally: Mason received Liberty Hall, and for Orlando he hired Gideon Shryock, designer of the Kentucky State Capitol, to design the Greek Revival Orlando Brown House. Liberty Hall opened as a museum in 1937 and was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1971. The map pin marks the house at 218 Wilkinson Street.

properties.name: Owingsville (Bath County seat)
properties.title: Owingsville (Bath County seat)
properties.subtitle: Bath County · US 60 at KY 36 · Owings’s iron furnaces from 1795 · town founded 1811
properties.history:
In 1795 Colonel Thomas Dye Owings was sent from Maryland to Kentucky by his father to operate some of the first iron furnaces in the region. Within fifteen years he had amassed a good deal of wealth and land. Owings and Colonel Richard H. Menefee each owned large parcels of the ground where the town would stand, and, as the story is told, the two men wagered that whoever built the finer home the quickest would give the community his name.

Owings won, and Owingsville was founded in 1811, the year Bath County was formed. It is the county seat, set roughly at the center of the county where US 60 meets KY 36. The map pin marks the town.

properties.name: Mann’s Lick saltworks (approximate, north of Fairdale)
properties.title: Mann’s Lick saltworks (approximate, north of Fairdale)
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County · near Manslick Road, north of Fairdale, Louisville · named 1773 · saltworks 1787 · fortified 1788 · Newtown 1794
properties.history:
Mann’s Lick was a salt lick just north of the present-day Fairdale neighborhood of Louisville. It was named for John Mann, a member of Captain Thomas Bullitt’s surveying party of 1773. The land was given to Colonel John Todd in 1780, and when Todd died at the Battle of Blue Licks in 1782 it passed to his daughter, Mary O. Todd.

Joseph Brooks, a Pennsylvanian who had worked at Bullitt’s Lick near Shepherdsville, leased it from her in 1787 and started a saltworks at once, building a hollow-log pipe to carry brine to his furnace; remains of the logs could still be seen in the 1940s. Fear of Indian attack led to fortifications around the works in 1788. Hundreds of workers, many of them enslaved, made the salt, and some settled on James F. Moore’s land nearby, leading to the 1794 charter of Newtown.

Sold under brands such as Little Sandy Salt, it was prized by merchants and sold as far away as Lexington; in 1808 it fetched $2 to $2.25 a bushel, and at its height the works ran around the clock. But the lick was smaller than Bullitt’s, and steamboats brought cheaper salt to Louisville; by 1830 the town and the salt had dwindled. Newcomers after 1910 renamed the area Fairdale, and Manslick Road keeps the old name. The map pin is an approximate point just north of Fairdale.

properties.name: Red River Gorge Geological Area
properties.title: Red River Gorge Geological Area
properties.subtitle: Menifee, Powell, and Wolfe counties · Daniel Boone National Forest · dam fight 1962–1993 · National Natural Landmark 1976
properties.history:
The Red River Gorge is a canyon system on the Red River in east-central Kentucky, part of the Pottsville Escarpment, carved over millions of years by erosion and weathering into high sandstone cliffs, rock shelters, waterfalls, and natural bridges. More than 100 natural sandstone arches stand in the gorge, the highest concentration of arches anywhere east of the Mississippi, and its rock shelters hold evidence of people from the Paleoindian period on, including early plant domestication.

In 1962 the “Great Flood of Clay City,” the worst in 102 years, led officials and local communities to press the state and the Kennedy administration for a flood-control dam, and the Army Corps of Engineers began planning one. Many people feared the reservoir would destroy the gorge’s unusual ecosystem, and the Sierra Club led the opposition. The struggle lasted decades and involved two proposed dam sites.

The gorge became a National Natural Landmark and National Archaeological District in 1976, and the fight ended on December 3, 1993, when President Bill Clinton signed the Red River Designation Act, adding the river to the National Wild and Scenic Rivers system and barring any dam. Today the roughly 29,000-acre Red River Gorge Geological Area lies within the Daniel Boone National Forest, beside Natural Bridge State Park.

The map pin marks the gorge in Menifee County; the geological area also reaches into Powell and Wolfe counties.

properties.name: Big Crossing Station / Great Crossing
properties.title: Big Crossing Station / Great Crossing
properties.subtitle: Scott County · buffalo ford on North Elkhorn · founded 1783 by Capt. Robert Johnson · Great Crossing Baptist Church
properties.history:
Robert Johnson (1745–1815) founded Johnson’s Station in 1783 at the bison ford on Elkhorn Creek in Scott County, the place called Great Crossing. The site was also called Great Buffalo Crossing and the Crossing, with Georgetown about three miles east. A post office operated there from 1811 to 1905.

The state marker at the community says he moved from Beargrass to Bryan’s Station in 1780, represented Fayette County in the Virginia Assembly, served as surveyor of Kentucky, and led frontier defense from 1787 to 1793. He was a trustee of Georgetown, a Scott County justice, sat in the Kentucky legislature in 1802, and was a member of both constitutional conventions, in 1792 and 1799.

Tradition on that marker holds that his wife, Jemima Suggett Johnson (1753–1814), led the women of Bryan’s Station to the spring for water just before the August 1782 siege. The Johnsons were charter members and land donors of Great Crossing Baptist Church. Three sons sat in Congress in 1825: Representatives James and John T. Johnson and Senator Richard M. Johnson, who became vice president in 1837. Robert and Jemima are buried in the church cemetery with five of their eleven children.

With John Craig he later gave the land for Wilmington, the Boone County town renamed Burlington. The map pin is Great Crossing on North Elkhorn.

properties.name: Campbellsville (Taylor County seat)
properties.title: Campbellsville (Taylor County seat)
properties.subtitle: Taylor County · Buckhorn Creek / Green River · town established 1817 · county seat 1848
properties.history:
Andrew Campbell of Augusta County, Virginia, was selling lots and keeping a gristmill and a tavern by 1814, and the legislature established Campbellsville in 1817. He laid the town out with his wife Rebecca and his brothers James, Adam, Michael, and David, on ground that was still in Green County. The state marker says the place was first settled about 1800, names Adam and Andrew among the founders, and records that Andrew died in 1819.

Taylor County, Kentucky’s 100th county, was cut from Green in 1848 and named for Gen. Zachary Taylor. Campbellsville became the seat, and the town sold the public square to the county for one dollar so a courthouse could be built. Taylor County has claimed the state’s geographic center, which the city motto repeats as the city in the middle of the commonwealth. The map pin marks the town.

properties.name: Siege of Boonesborough (Sept 1778)
properties.title: Siege of Boonesborough (Sept 1778)
properties.subtitle: Madison County · Fort Boonesborough · Blackfish (Cot-ta-wa-ma-go) · eleven-day Shawnee siege
properties.history:
Blackfish (c. 1729–1779), war chief of the Chillicothe Shawnee, refused to give up Kentucky hunting ground after Dunmore’s War. Shawnee leaders such as Cornstalk had accepted the Ohio River as a boundary. Blackfish did not. In the Revolution, British officials at Detroit encouraged and supplied raids meant to push settlers back north of the river.

On February 7, 1778, after Cornstalk’s murder at Fort Randolph, Blackfish captured Daniel Boone and the men with him at the salt springs on the Licking River, the place Kentuckians call the Blue Licks. Boone persuaded the outnumbered party to surrender.

At Chillicothe, near present Xenia, Ohio, he was adopted into a Shawnee family and named Sheltowee, “Big Turtle.” Tradition says Blackfish himself adopted him; historian John Sugden has suggested another family. Boone escaped in June 1778, when he learned a large force was coming, and warned Boonesborough.

On September 7, 1778, Blackfish reached Boonesborough with a force Boone counted as 444 Native warriors, mostly Shawnee, with Cherokee, Wyandot, Miami, Delaware, and Mingo allies, and 12 French-Canadian militia. The siege was lifted on September 18, after eleven days. Col. Richard Callaway, who defended the fort and later charged Boone, has his own story here. Boone was acquitted.

The next spring Col. John Bowman led Kentucky militia against Chillicothe. Blackfish helped hold the town and was shot in the leg. The wound became infected and killed him. Chillicothe stood in present Ohio and is not pinned here. The map pin is the Boonesborough siege site.

properties.name: Burlington (Boone County seat)
properties.title: Burlington (Boone County seat)
properties.subtitle: Boone County · Craig’s Camp / Wilmington 1800 · renamed Burlington 1816 · unincorporated county seat
properties.history:
In June 1799 Boone County’s first court fixed the county seat at Craig’s Camp, 74 acres at the headwaters of Allens Fork. The camp was named for John Hawkins Craig. The next year John Craig and Robert Johnson, who has his own story here, gave 74 acres at the Woolper Creek site for a town they called Wilmington.

Court sat in a log courthouse in January 1801, and the town was platted that September. County surveyor Moses Scott laid the streets around a central Public Square; two roads later cut through the square.

In 1816 the U.S. Post Office asked for a new name, and Burlington stuck. The town was incorporated in 1824 and lost its charter in 1923. It remains one of Kentucky’s two unincorporated county seats, with Whitley City in McCreary County. The 1889 Renaissance Revival courthouse, by the McDonald brothers, still stands, and the Burlington Historic District was listed in 1979. The map pin marks the town.

properties.name: Camp Nelson USCT recruiting and training center
properties.title: Camp Nelson USCT recruiting and training center
properties.subtitle: Jessamine County · Camp Nelson National Monument · USCT recruiting 1864–1865 · eight regiments · Nov. 1864 expulsion · March 3, 1865 joint resolution
properties.history:
President Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation of January 1, 1863, applied only to areas in rebellion. Kentucky had stayed in the Union, so the proclamation did not free anyone held in slavery there. In February 1863 the Kentucky General Assembly resolved that the state would not accept emancipation, compensated or otherwise.

By 1864 white enlistment in Kentucky had fallen, and the Army began recruiting Black Kentuckians. For an enslaved man, enlistment brought his freedom. By early summer 1864 the remaining limits were lifted, and Camp Nelson, the Jessamine County supply depot founded in 1863 that has its own story here, became one of eight training centers for U.S. Colored Troops (USCT) in the state.

Recruiting at Camp Nelson began in early June 1864. Eight USCT regiments were organized there: the 114th, 116th, 119th and 124th Colored Infantry, the 5th and 6th Colored Cavalry, and the 12th and 13th Colored Heavy Artillery. On July 25, 1864, 322 men joined the 12th Heavy Artillery, the camp’s largest single day of USCT enlistment.

Enslaved men who set out for Camp Nelson to enlist faced violence on the way. Some were whipped or mutilated, with ears cut off, and mobs attacked recruit columns. On May 23, 1864, Danville residents threw stones and fired pistols at about 250 Boyle County recruits marching to the camp. In Adair County a man turned away from enlisting was severely whipped when he returned home, and in Taylor County some recruits were beaten and jailed.

The opposition had several roots. Many white Kentuckians had backed the Union on the expectation that slavery would survive, and Black enlistment deepened their resentment. Slavery was still legal in the state, so local officials could treat a man headed to camp as a runaway. In March 1865 the Lexington night-watch captain arrested William Jones and his wife on the road to Camp Nelson, took their savings and sent them back to their enslaver; Jones escaped again and enlisted in the 124th.

The National Park Service ranks Camp Nelson as the largest USCT recruiting center in Kentucky and the third largest in the nation. The 116th served in the siege of Petersburg and the Appomattox campaign. The 5th and 6th Cavalry rode on raids into southwestern Virginia, including fights at Saltville and Marion. The 124th, organized for volunteers with physical infirmities and for young boys, did garrison duty in Kentucky.

Families who came with the recruits had no such path to freedom. Wives and children of Kentucky soldiers were still legally enslaved, and the Army repeatedly ordered them out of camp. On November 23, 1864, on the order of camp commander Brig. Gen. Speed S. Fry, soldiers loaded more than 400 women and children onto wagons, drove them beyond the lines in a winter storm, and destroyed their huts.

Fry’s superiors quickly rescinded the order. Of those expelled, about 250 returned to Camp Nelson, and at least 102 of them died in the following weeks and months of exposure and illness. What became of the roughly 150 who did not return is not known. The expulsion drew newspaper coverage across the country and reached Congress.

The Army opened a Home for Colored Refugees at the camp in January 1865. On March 3, 1865, a joint resolution of Congress (13 Stat. 571) freed the wives and children of men serving in the USCT. Until the 13th Amendment, that measure was the only way most Black refugees in Kentucky could become legally free.

The Kentucky General Assembly rejected the 13th Amendment on February 24, 1865. It took effect nationally when three-fourths of the states ratified it on December 6, 1865, and only then did slavery end in Kentucky. By that time 23,703 Black men had enlisted in Kentucky, more than 10,000 of them in regiments organized at Camp Nelson.

Kentucky ratified the amendment symbolically in 1976. The map pin marks the Camp Nelson National Monument visitor center.

properties.name: Buck Pond / Col. Thomas Marshall
properties.title: Buck Pond / Col. Thomas Marshall
properties.subtitle: Woodford County · Buck Pond (c. 1783) · Virginia surveyor general of military lands · private horse farm
properties.history:
Col. Thomas Marshall (1730–1802) came to Kentucky as a veteran of two wars and a surveyor by trade. Born in Westmoreland County, Virginia, he is best remembered as the father of Chief Justice John Marshall. In the Revolution he was colonel of the 3rd Virginia Regiment of the Continental Army.

His regiment fought at Brandywine, covered the Continental retreat at Germantown, and wintered with Washington at Valley Forge. Ordered south, Marshall was among the troops surrendered at Charleston in 1780. While on parole he rode over the mountains to Kentucky for the first time and located the land he would later settle.

In 1783 he was appointed surveyor general of the Kentucky lands due to the officers and soldiers of Virginia’s Continental Line, and he opened his office in Lexington. Virginia had promised its veterans land instead of cash, and his office was where those promises became surveyed tracts. That made him one of the men who decided how the Bluegrass would be divided among its new owners.

Buck Pond Farm’s own history dates his farm near present Versailles to 1783 and the house to 1785. He moved the rest of his family from Fauquier County, Virginia, to Kentucky in 1785. The farm’s account says George Washington appointed him surveyor general of the lands of Fayette County, but Washington was not yet president in 1783; another account credits Washington only with naming him Kentucky’s collector of revenue later.

Fayette County voters sent Marshall to the Virginia House of Delegates for the 1787–1788 session. In 1788 he was also a delegate to the convention at Danville that weighed Kentucky’s separation from Virginia, and his family were Federalists. Around 1800 he turned Buck Pond over to his youngest son, Dr. Louis Marshall, and he died in Mason County in 1802.

Marshall opposed slavery in Ohio but practiced and proposed indentured servitude for formerly enslaved people. Neither source says who labored at Buck Pond in his lifetime, so that part of the farm’s story is still untold here.

## Kentucky today

Buck Pond is still a Thoroughbred farm on Paynes Mill Road outside Versailles, and the farm says six generations of Marshalls lived there under the Revolutionary grant. Later owners bred the 1902 Kentucky Derby winner Alan-a-Dale and raised Spectacular Bid there. The farm is private and welcomes visitors by appointment only, so the map pin is for viewing from the road.

properties.name: Prestonsburg founding / Preston’s Station
properties.title: Prestonsburg founding / Preston’s Station
properties.subtitle: Floyd County seat · Preston’s Station 1797 · Floyd County 1800 · established 1818
properties.history:
Prestonsburg sits on the Levisa Fork of the Big Sandy, on land that was part of a 100,000-acre colonial grant to the family of Elizabeth Patton Preston. Her husband, John Preston, managed the grant on her behalf. The grant was meant to open land beyond the Blue Ridge to British settlement, but French and Native resistance and a change in British policy kept it from doing much for decades.

No one settled the tract until John Spurlock of Montgomery County, Virginia, arrived in 1791. He laid out the town of Preston’s Station in 1797. The Kentucky Secretary of State’s city record says the name was later changed to honor Col. John Preston, the landowner.

On December 13, 1799, the General Assembly created Floyd County, effective June 1, 1800, from parts of Fleming, Montgomery and Mason counties. It was named for the surveyor John Floyd, and Preston’s Station became its seat.

On April 8, 1808, the first courthouse burned and took the early records with it, so Floyd County’s surviving government records begin in 1808. The post office was called Floyd Court House from 1816 until the late 1820s. The town itself was formally established in 1818.

Some popular histories credit a surveyor named John Graham with the 1797 plat and give a May 3, 1797 date. The sources checked here name John Spurlock and give no day, so this story leaves both points open.

## Kentucky today

Prestonsburg is still the Floyd County seat. The Samuel May House, built in 1817 and now owned by the city, is the Big Sandy Valley’s oldest known brick home, and Confederate units recruited there in the Civil War. Nearby Middle Creek was the largest Civil War battle in eastern Kentucky, fought January 10, 1862.

properties.name: Old Forester / Whiskey Row (Louisville)
properties.title: Old Forester / Whiskey Row (Louisville)
properties.subtitle: Jefferson County · Whiskey Row, W. Main St. · George Garvin Brown · first sealed-bottle bourbon 1870
properties.history:
George Garvin Brown was born in Munfordville on September 2, 1846, and moved to Louisville in 1862. He went to Male High School and started out as a wholesale drug salesman. That trade taught him something about the whiskey business: doctors and pharmacists bought it as medicine and needed to trust what was in the bottle.

In Brown’s day, distillers shipped their whiskey in barrels, casks and kegs. Bars and grocers bought it wholesale and sold it in their own bottles, and some watered or doctored it before they did. This hurt customers, the doctors who prescribed whiskey, and the distillers whose names were attached to it.

In 1870 Brown and his half-brother, J. T. S. Brown Jr., started J. T. S. Brown and Brothers. Their answer was Old Forester, sold only in sealed glass bottles so that no one between the distillery and the buyer could tamper with it. Brown signed every label as his guarantee and trademarked the name, and he first sold it through pharmacies.

Where the name came from is disputed. The usual account says it honored a Louisville physician, Dr. William Forrester, which may explain the early two-“r” spelling. Other sources name Confederate general Nathan Bedford Forrest instead, and no one knows for sure why the spelling changed.

Brown’s bookkeeper, George Forman, became his partner, and in 1890 the firm took the name Brown-Forman. Brown was the first president of the National Liquor Dealers’ Association in 1894 and wrote a book against Prohibition in 1910. He died in 1917 and is buried in Louisville’s Cave Hill Cemetery.

During Prohibition, Old Forester was one of six Kentucky brands bottled under federal permits for medicinal use. A generation after Brown’s first bottles, the 1897 Bottled-in-Bond Act put a federal guarantee behind some whiskey labels too. Brown’s company and the first commercially bottled bourbon are one of many bourbon “firsts” that historians still argue over.

## Kentucky today

Old Forester is now distilled on Louisville’s Whiskey Row, at 119 West Main Street, the company’s home in the 1880s. Brown-Forman is still headquartered in Louisville and is still controlled by Brown’s descendants. Like Evan Williams on the wharf and Frederick Stitzel’s barrel racks, Brown’s idea helped make Louisville a center of the bourbon trade.

properties.name: Sassafras Ridge (15Fu3), Fulton County (approximate)
properties.title: Sassafras Ridge (15Fu3), Fulton County (approximate)
properties.subtitle: Fulton County · Mississippian mound center · ~AD 1000–1500 · address restricted
properties.history:
Sassafras Ridge (site 15Fu3) is a Mississippian mound center in Fulton County. The National Register of Historic Places lists periods of significance reaching back to AD 0, with the Mississippian centuries of AD 1000–1499 the latest. Mississippian is the name archaeologists give a way of life, not a tribe, and the people who lived here left no name for themselves that has come down to us.

Mississippian towns were built by farming communities that grew corn and raised earthen platform mounds around open plazas. Archaeologist R. Barry Lewis studied Sassafras Ridge with the Adams site, also in Fulton County in a 1986 report for the Kentucky Heritage Council. He treated the three as a group of towns in Fulton County.

The site is listed on the National Register for what it can still teach, and its exact location is restricted to protect it from looting. Our map pin is rounded to about 10 kilometers. Please do not go looking for it; the site is not open to the public.

A 2019 federal notice covered a fragment of human bone picked up from the mound’s surface in 1978. Western Kentucky University found no cultural affiliation with any present-day tribe, which is a reminder that the people of Mississippian towns cannot be matched to a single modern nation.

## Kentucky today

Visitors can see a Mississippian town of the same era at Wickliffe Mounds State Historic Site in Ballard County. Fulton County later became part of the Jackson Purchase, bought from the Chickasaw in 1818, centuries after Sassafras Ridge was abandoned.

properties.name: Hartford / Fort Hartford (Rough River)
properties.title: Hartford / Fort Hartford (Rough River)
properties.subtitle: Ohio County seat · Fort Hartford c. 1782 · county seat 1799 · incorporated 1808
properties.history:
Hartford sits on a bluff above the Rough River, a long tributary of the Green River that early settlers called Rough Creek. The land was part of a 4,000-acre Virginia grant to Gabriel Madison, and it was surveyed in 1782. The state historical marker for Fort Hartford says there is evidence of a settlement here that same year, the first fortified place in the lower Green River Valley.

The frontiersman William Smeathers later wrote that he and other settlers helped build “a fort at Hartford on Rough Creek” in 1782–83. Local tradition calls it the first permanent settlement in Ohio County. The stockade and its small log buildings are believed to have stood on the bluff where the town’s water plant is today.

The marker also says the fort was “often scene of bloody strife with Indians.” Shawnee and other nations north of the Ohio had never accepted the loss of their Kentucky hunting grounds, and to them stations like this one were an invasion. In April 1790 raiders struck nearby Barnett’s Station, killing two children and carrying off ten-year-old Hannah Barnett, who was held captive for six months.

The General Assembly created Ohio County in December 1798 from Hardin County and named it for the Ohio River, then its northern border. The county marker dates the first county court to 1799, and Hartford became the seat after Madison gave land for the town. Its first public building, a two-story log courthouse and jail, went up in 1799–1800.

That courthouse had a raised bench for the court and a rail for the lawyers, but it collapsed in 1813. According to the First Public Building marker, the salvaged timber was burned to celebrate Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry’s victory on Lake Erie. The post office opened as Hartford Court House in 1801, and the legislature incorporated the town in 1808.

No one is sure where the name came from. The Fort Hartford marker says it comes from the river ford where animals crossed, and “hart” is an old word for a male deer. Other accounts point to an early settler who ran a ferry here, and travelers used the ford or a ferry until the first covered bridge across the Rough River was built in 1823.

properties.name: Chambers Site (15Ml109), Marshall County (approximate)
properties.title: Chambers Site (15Ml109), Marshall County (approximate)
properties.subtitle: Marshall County · Mississippian village · Angelly phase ~AD 1250–1350 · location restricted
properties.history:
The Chambers site (15Ml109) is a Mississippian village in Marshall County. It covers about six hectares, close to fifteen acres, and a stone-box cemetery was reported there. Mississippian is the name archaeologists give a way of life, not a tribe, and the villagers left no name for themselves that has come down to us.

Archaeologists learned of the site by accident in the mid-1980s, when construction work cut into it. David Pollack and Jimmy A. Railey of the Kentucky Heritage Council recorded what the construction had exposed and published their report in 1987. A suite of radiocarbon dates suggests the village was lived in from about AD 1250 to 1350.

At the edge of the cut they found two houses built with wall trenches, one about 5 by 6.4 meters and the other about 6 by 8 meters. Downslope lay a trash area some 10 by 16 meters. Test units went through more than a meter of Mississippian deposits, including the edges of a series of prepared floors and thick, dark midden.

Pollack and Railey thought the floors belonged to a terrace or bench that held a series of houses or outdoor work areas, swept and rebuilt again and again. Archaeologist R. Berle Clay later argued that they had clipped the edge of a low platform mound instead. The question is still open, and a mound would make Chambers more than an ordinary village.

The people of Chambers grew maize, gathered nuts, and raised native crops such as maygrass in larger amounts than other sites in the region. They ate far less fish and fewer migrating birds than people at large river-valley towns. Their hoes were made of both Dover chert, quarried in Tennessee, and Mill Creek chert from southern Illinois.

Its pottery places Chambers in what archaeologists call the Angelly phase, with loop handles rather than the wide strap handles of later times. Serving bowls were less common than at big mound towns such as the Adams site, while cooking pans were more common. Chambers and Jonathan Creek are the best-defined Angelly phase communities in this part of Kentucky.

Kentucky today: Chambers is not a public site, and our map pin is rounded to about 10 kilometers to protect it from looting, so please do not go looking for it. The later Mississippian town at Tinsley Hill, in Lyon County, shows how these communities changed after Chambers was abandoned.

properties.name: Yahoo Falls, Big South Fork (McCreary County)
properties.title: Yahoo Falls, Big South Fork (McCreary County)
properties.subtitle: McCreary County · ~113-ft plunge · Yahoo Falls Recreation Area 1960s · Big South Fork NRRA 1987
properties.history:
Yahoo Falls is a single plunge of about 113 feet on Yahoo Creek in McCreary County, inside the Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area. The National Park Service calls it Kentucky’s highest waterfall. A falls in the Red River Gorge is said to beat it by a few inches, so the title is friendly ground for argument.

The creek pours off a sandstone ledge on the Cumberland Plateau in front of one of the park’s largest rock houses, a shallow cave worn back under the cliff. Hikers can walk right up to the base and even behind the falling water. In late summer the falls can shrink to a trickle, and it runs best after spring rain.

The falls lie in timberland that became part of the Cumberland National Forest when it was created in 1937; the forest was renamed the Daniel Boone National Forest in 1968. In the 1960s forest supervisor Robert Collins set out to make Yahoo Falls an easy scenic stop that would draw visitors to the Stearns Ranger District. Crews built a road to the top of the gorge, a picnic area and campsite, trails, and a long flight of steel stairs down past the cliffs.

In 1987 the land passed from the Forest Service to the National Park Service as part of Big South Fork. The 1960s picnic shelter still stands, and the Park Service restored it in 2011 with help from inmates at the nearby federal penitentiary. McCreary County and the Park Service paved the road to the falls in 2016.

No one is sure how the falls got its name, which is also spelled Ywahoo and may come from a Muscogee word. Several local legends about the name and about frontier events at the falls are often repeated, but none has been traced to records from the time, so they are left out here.

Kentucky today: To reach the falls, take KY 700 off U.S. 27 at Whitley City and follow the road to the Yahoo Falls picnic area and trailhead. A loop of about a mile reaches the base, the steep metal stairs can be hard for some hikers, and a spur leads to the 100-foot-long Yahoo Arch, according to Kentucky Tourism. Cumberland Falls is a short drive to the northeast.

properties.name: Walker Daniel marker, Danville (KHS #190)
properties.title: Walker Daniel marker, Danville (KHS #190)
properties.subtitle: Boyle County · Danville laid out 1783 · first District attorney general · killed 1784 · town named 1787
properties.history:
Danville is named for Walker Daniel, a young Virginia lawyer who came to central Kentucky in 1781 and laid out the town at Crow’s Station in 1783. One man who knew him called him “a young gentleman of rare talents” who “gave promise of great distinction.” In 1782 he bought land from John Crow, founder of Crow’s Station, near present Danville.

In 1783, Kentucky was still part of Virginia, and the new District of Kentucky needed its own court. Daniel was appointed the district’s first attorney general, its chief prosecutor. He “laid off a part of seventy-six acres for a town” at Crow’s Station and gave land for the court, where a crude two-room log courthouse and a jail of hewn logs “at least nine inches thick” were built.

The district court soon moved to the public square that became Constitution Square, where the conventions that led to statehood would meet. In 1784 Daniel wrote to Virginia Governor Benjamin Harrison that Kentuckians wanted a separate state. He blamed what he called “the cruelties & Depredations of the Savages” and argued that a Kentucky government would care more about keeping peace with its Native neighbors than distant Virginia did.

Those neighbors saw the war very differently: Shawnee and other nations north of the Ohio were fighting to keep settlers off hunting grounds they had never agreed to give up. Dividing up that land was part of Daniel’s own work. Daniel served on the commission at the Falls of the Ohio that allotted land in George Rogers Clark’s grant to the soldiers of the Illinois Regiment. In August 1784 he set out from the Falls toward his brother’s place at Bullitt’s Lick.

About six miles from the saltworks, a party of about seven warriors attacked Daniel and two companions. A Virginia newspaper reported that Daniel and a man named Keightly were killed on the spot, and that a third man, Johnston, escaped with a wound across his chest. The attackers took scalps but left the men’s money and clothes.

Daniel’s brother Robert sold the rest of the town lots and placed the springs in trust for the townspeople. In 1787 the Virginia act that formally established the town recognized the lots Walker Daniel had laid off “in his lifetime,” and the town was named Danville in his honor.

## Kentucky today

Danville is the Boyle County seat, and state historical marker #190 for Walker Daniel stands at Second and Main streets, near Constitution Square. Nearby markers tell of John Crow’s station and the district court where Daniel served as prosecutor.

properties.name: Father David Rice home marker, Greensburg (KHS #844)
properties.title: Father David Rice home marker, Greensburg (KHS #844)
properties.subtitle: Green County · Presbyterian minister · Greensburg home c. 1798–1816
properties.history:
State historical marker #844 in Greensburg marks the home of the Rev. David Rice, called Father Rice, who organized the first Presbyterian churches west of the Alleghenies in 1784. Born in Virginia in 1733, he came to Kentucky in 1783, founded Rice's School, or Transylvania Seminary, near Danville in 1785 and urged gradual emancipation at the 1792 constitutional convention.

The marker says he came to the Greensburg area in 1798 and formed two churches here; a Danville church history dates his move to Green County to 1793. He died in 1816 and is buried at Danville.

properties.name: La Grange courthouse square and Main Street tracks
properties.title: La Grange courthouse square and Main Street tracks
properties.subtitle: Oldham County seat · laid out 1827 · permanent seat 1838 · incorporated 1840
properties.history:
La Grange was laid out in 1827 where the Shelbyville–Westport road crossed the Louisville–New Castle road, on land surveyor William Berry Taylor donated. It was named for Lafayette's French estate. The Oldham County court moved here in 1827, returned to Westport, and settled in La Grange for good in 1838; the town was incorporated in 1840.

In the 1850s the Louisville and Frankfort Railroad laid its tracks straight down Main Street, and freight trains still run between the shops today.

properties.name: Remember the Raisin: Kentucky volunteers' muster, Georgetown (KHS #508)
properties.title: Remember the Raisin: Kentucky volunteers' muster, Georgetown (KHS #508)
properties.subtitle: Scott County · muster Aug 15, 1812 · River Raisin Jan 1813
properties.history:
Kentucky volunteers mustered on the Georgetown courthouse lawn on August 15, 1812, ordered north toward Detroit. In January 1813 they took Frenchtown on the River Raisin, in present Monroe, Michigan, but on January 22 British troops, Canadian militia and about 800 warriors led by the Wyandot chiefs Roundhead and Walk-in-the-Water defeated them. The next day warriors killed an estimated 30 to 60 wounded prisoners, an event Americans called a massacre.

Of about 1,050 Kentuckians, the marker says, not half reached home. Nine Kentucky counties are named for officers lost in the campaign.

properties.name: C. and O. Mounds, Johnson County (approximate)
properties.title: C. and O. Mounds, Johnson County (approximate)
properties.subtitle: Johnson County · Adena burial mounds · Early Woodland · location generalized
properties.history:
In Johnson County, Adena people raised two burial mounds about 1,600 feet apart, each over circular rings of paired posts. William S. Webb's University of Kentucky crews excavated them with Works Progress Administration support and published them in 1942.

Webb read each mound as the grave of an important person over a house, with small hamlets nearby. Later work has not found those villages, and many archaeologists now see the post circles as ceremonial structures. The sites are not public; this pin is generalized to about 10 km.

properties.name: Maysville–Lexington Turnpike (US 68), Maysville Hill (KHS #144)
properties.title: Maysville–Lexington Turnpike (US 68), Maysville Hill (KHS #144)
properties.subtitle: Mason County · turnpike chartered 1829 · Jackson veto 1830 · opened to Lexington 1835
properties.history:
The road from Maysville through Washington and Paris to Lexington began as a buffalo trace and settler path. A turnpike company was chartered in 1829, and in 1830 Congress voted to buy $150,000 of its stock, but on May 27, 1830, President Andrew Jackson vetoed the bill, calling the road a local project.

Kentucky built it anyway. The first four miles, Maysville to Washington, were finished in November 1830 as the earliest macadamized road west of the Alleghenies, and the road opened to Lexington in 1835 with thirteen tollhouses. US 68 follows it today.
